#6435. The Best New Restaurants in America in 2026

The year’s top restaurant debuts give us infinite reasons to dine out right now

These are the 15 new restaurants that best captured the year in dining. Our team of editors and scouts traveled across the country, drawing on years of experience to build the 2026 winners list.

What we found remarkable: the quiet confidence of a chef who’s mastered Hungarian food in Pittsburgh; a fresh revamp of family-style Italian dining in Philadelphia grounded in the original restaurant’s 1950s roots; a cozy tribute to Southern cuisine in Denver that still manages to feel cool. What they have in common: a sincere commitment to making diners feel at home. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

“You went to Kansas City for sushi?” I was asked more than once — with some derision — after returning from Missouri, so I can only imagine the uphill battle chef Peter Hoang faces at Akoya Omakase. Hoang isn’t easily daunted. He’s so committed to sourcing, he often personally drives to the airport to pick up the fish hand-selected by his two private buyers in Tokyo 26 hours after placing his order.

At Akoya, the fish quality is unassailable; the rice seasoned with precision. But Hoang consistently finds ways to complement Akoya’s sashimi and nigiri with unexpected accents. Smoky juvenile king mackerel gets a hit of acid and sweetness from pineapple chutney. Truffle, notorious for being overwhelming on just about anything, manifests in pate form alongside dashi and kelp salt to highlight delicate hirame. The miso-butter-accented crab nigiri (a steal at $6) calls to mind decadently dipping crab legs in drawn butter. While affordable for omakase, $165 is still a commitment: Akoya diners have the option to test the waters with a la carte offerings and lunch specials in a warm and unpretentious restaurant. Befitting the Midwestern stereotype, the personable chefs, who chat freely with those seated across the bar, are eager to answer questions. Even tables in the dining room chime in.

Hoang, who worked in his father’s mid-2000s sushi restaurant before heading to bigger markets like New York and Chicago, is excited to be part of his hometown’s emerging Japanese dining scene — one that’s increasingly drawing national attention thanks to ambitious restaurants like Anjin izakaya and promising newcomers like day-to-night Tian Tea House/Moon Bar. Kansas City just might develop a reputation for cuisine beyond barbecue. — MF

Assuming new ownership of beloved, old restaurants can be a risk, but South Philly local Joey Baldino has the formula down: Keep the trappings, dial in the food. After taking over his family’s private Palizzi Social Club and retaining its members-only allure, Baldino bought Bomb Bomb Bar, which first opened in 1951, and reopened it last year. The bar’s lore precedes it: A rival business bombed it twice, immortalized by the large neon sign of two cartoonish bombs. Some reboots feel ironic, but not this one; the payphone by the door, the swordfish on the wall, and even the endearingly gruff servers feel like they’ve been there forever. It’s proof that classic Philly and modern culinary destination Philly can coexist.

In the front room, locals analyze Eagles games, and you might hear children playing in the street. In the back dining room, the procession of seafood here, priced at $65 per person, feels like a steal in this era of rising prices. The meat for the lobster Française has been removed from its shell, battered and fried, placed onto a buttery sauce, and then crowned with its shell once more. The crispy calamari gets enlivened with twangy cherry peppers. But it’s the overall dining experience that’s unbeatable: The restaurant hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but as the Beach Boys play and you sip a pepperoncini martini while watching your server pour hot fudge onto a sundae, you remember (perhaps while still wearing a bib) that complete novelty isn’t always necessary. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Cassis is big in every sense. The nearly 200-seat dining room of the Milwaukee restaurant is an immaculately designed jewel box of gleaming tile, cozy banquettes, and antique mirrors, and even on a Wednesday night, it’s packed and roaring, with a towering, glowing bar at the center of the action. The latest project from Kyle and Meghan Knall, the couple behind nearby acclaimed bistro Birch, channels the conviviality and polish of a classic, old-world French brasserie while remaining distinctly Midwestern in spirit. It’s an all-day restaurant with both heart and panache.

Kyle Knall’s cooking roots itself in French tradition without feeling stodgy or like Parisian cosplay. Instead, it takes cues from his farm-to-table approach at Birch: Classical technique provides a framework for showing off Wisconsin ingredients with playfulness, vividness, and attention to detail. Oeuf mayo gets a jolt from intensely herbaceous, bright green aioli; ravioli Dauphiné pairs almost sugary-sweet summer corn with buttery Wisconsin-made Pleasant Ridge Reserve cheese; and an understated, frill-free but deeply umami foie gras eclair transforms one of French cuisine’s richest ingredients into an almost weightless bite.

At a moment when ambitious dining often means intimate tasting-menu counters and an air of exclusivity, Cassis makes a case that dinner can still feel like a real night out on the town. The cooking has an eagerness to please that succeeds. Within its walls, you’re offered an increasingly rare pleasure: a space where you’re invited to settle in, linger, order another bottle of wine, and maybe even have a friendly chat with the table next to you. Cassis could exist — and surely thrive — in New York or Las Vegas, but it’s more exciting in Milwaukee, where its scale and ambition feel like a vote of confidence in the city itself. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor, Eater

In 2026, the Midwest has proven a formidable destination for dining, with restaurants from Cleveland to Milwaukee leaning into what makes the region’s food special. Creepies in Chicago embodies this movement: A nonsensical (if memorable) name belies a thoughtful restaurant destination from chefs David and Anna Posey. The refreshing space feels contemporary, but with cottage-esque touches — geometric patterns dot the furniture, cartoonish artwork shares space with kitchenware tchotchkes, and mini curtains hang from open shelving.

Chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski embeds French technique into dishes fiercely grounded in Chicago’s identity. Steamed mussels get kissed with classic Pernod and a fennel giardiniera that honors the city’s iconic Italian beef sandwiches. An Alsatian-leaning tarte flambe comes “tavern-style,” a nod to the square-cut pizza beloved by locals. Not every dish invokes the Great Lakes; the generous portion of gougeres may be Midwest-appropriate, but here the French classic takes a decadent turn as warm Brie seeps from the center of each choux pastry. A textbook roast chicken’s umami-laden sauce gains extra depth from liver; drag one of the restaurant’s hefty, yet impossibly crispy fries through its drippings for the best bite of the night. Save room for Anna Posey’s desserts: The savory soft-serve trend manifests as a baguette-infused concoction topped with chocolate and buttery breadcrumbs. In a year when a diner can grow weary that Everything’s a Bistro these days, Creepies proves some still offer delights and surprises. — MF

I’ve always felt a connection to Cuban cuisine, having visited the island country in my youth and eaten many pan con lechons from LA’s Porto’s Bakery in iconic Glendale. But a July meal at Emelina, which snagged a Michelin star months after opening for its ambitious, $275 Cuban tasting menu, showed me the country’s cooking in an entirely new context.

I wasn’t the only one to find it a revelation. Several older Cubans fortunate enough to nab a reservation got emotional toward the end of the meal, moved to tears as they told me they’d never had Cuban food like this before.

Located in tony West Palm Beach, this striking restaurant from chefs Osmel González and Camila Salazar draws inspiration from the former’s family history and upbringing in Cuba. After working together at world-class restaurants like Disfrutar in Spain and SingleThread in California, they partnered with Alvaro Perez-Miranda to achieve their vision. Employing lush ingredients sourced from South Florida farms in Redland and Lake Worth, the meal starts with a tender knob of fried flounder topped with caviar — a winking nod to traditional pan con minuta, a fried fish sandwich slathered with tartar sauce. A mid-course of pristine tropical fruits including mamey, lychee, and mango, arranged over creamy ricotta and dotted with Benton’s country ham, conjures a bounty one might linger over on a Cuban beach. Rabo encendido, or braised oxtail with Koshihikari rice, takes the homestyle guisado to new heights.

Cuba has a long history of home restaurants called paladares, serving personalized versions of staple dishes like arroz con pollo. Emelina represents that same opportunity to delight and enlighten, casting attention on a cuisine and culture that could have been. In balmy West Palm Beach, it thrives. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

The winding walkway into Maroon is a portal into a new dimension, a leap from the beeps and bloops of the casino floor at the Sahara Las Vegas into a thrumming dining room, dimly lit and streaked with red-orange accents. Chef Kwame Onwuachi, who most recently earned acclaim at Tatiana in New York City and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., has become a beacon of African diasporic dishes in the middle of the Mojave Desert.

Onwuachi is building something approachable yet grounded in technique. The name Maroon comes from 17th- and 18th-century enslaved people who escaped and established mountain communities in Jamaica; the kitchen centers African and Caribbean flavors rooted in their foodways. Consider the artful array of bluefin tuna belly chunks, hamachi, and braised octopus, swimming in a tangy broth pool and best enjoyed spooned onto fried saltine crackers, that gets an intense but brief spice hit from Scotch bonnet peppers. Luxurious, palm-sized oxtail patties and jerk mushroom earn a dash of caviar and grated truffle, a maximalist garnish on the typically humble dish. Grilled butterflied shrimp brushed with achiote sofrito recall pescado zarandeado, while sweet white grape chow chow brings a puckery kick. The blackened jerk chicken, its juiciness sealed in with a crust of aromatic spices, might be the finest in the U.S.; oxtail fried rice could moonlight as Caribbean bibimbap, with saucy deboned beef and fork-tender stewed chicken on an assemblage of julienned peppers and peas. Yes, there is steak, but go for the seared, bone-in pork chop instead for its sweet glaze.

Maroon engages you with sensory brilliance and familiar yet indelible flavors, like a catchy song that gets better with each listen. In a different city, it might feel overwrought, but here in Las Vegas, it matches the city’s frenetic energy and lands like a satisfying opus. — MK

Maydan Market opened in 2025 as a collaborative restaurant space and marketplace home to a few different Los Angeles-born businesses; in essence, it functions as one super-incubator for some of the best food you can find in the city. Diners bounce around to try a pozole flight and pescadillas (sofrito-fried fish nested in supple blue corn tortillas) at Maléna, from the family behind the beloved Tamales Elena; a crisp, UFO-sized, asiento-painted tlayuda from Lugya’h, from Los Angeles legend Poncho’s Tlayudas; and chile-sauce-slicked gai tod from Golden Mountain Chicken (formerly Yhing Yhang), from the intrepid team behind Thai restaurant Holy Basil. They will certainly stop to perch at the rotating Club 104 stall, which has hosted Black-owned businesses such as Melnificent Wingz and Caribbean diasporic pop-up Rubie, as well as Palestinian home restaurant Mid East Eats. On their way out, they may circle the storefront simply named Sook to eye wines, spices, and woven goods sourced from the Levant.

This is not to mention the market’s anchor restaurants: the Lebanese-influenced Maydan and Compass Rose, respectable D.C. transplants from prolific restaurateur Rose Previte, who, alongside her team, curated the market with the knockout lineup of Indigenous vendors. Maydan Market feels boldly like one whole; people rarely come for a single hyped stall. The point, in effect, is the crawl. In a year marked by ongoing, unrelenting, nationwide ICE raids targeting Black and brown immigrants, the fact that the market centers Indigenous Mexican-owned businesses, allowing their owners the space and sovereignty to reach a wider stage and audience, speaks loudly. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Take the former location of Portland’s — if not North America’s — most famous Northern Thai restaurant, combine it with the city’s most prolific and highly decorated Thai chef and restaurateur in Akkapong “Earl” Ninsom, and pepper in an elite local bar manager — co-owner Eric Nelson. Mix it all together, and you get OK Chicken & Khao Soi. Those familiar with its predecessor, Pok Pok, will find the space uncannily similar: a covered patio and downstairs service at a small bar, upstairs seating at oilcloth-wrapped tables. Now customers order on paper tabs. It’s casual and intimate, with just the right level of noise to feel like you stumbled into a really good dinner party.

OK Chicken’s menu leans into the flavors of Chiang Mai, starting with crispy chicken wings and two styles of khao soi — one with chicken and another richly prepared with beef. Plates of smoky nam prik makheua (eggplant dip) come with crisp and waxy long beans, green cabbage leaves, and cucumber. A memorable dish of yum moo yang — tender grilled pork shoulder tossed with snappish chunks of celery stalk and leaves as well as sliced onion — relaxes in a funky fish sauce with Thai chiles that sneakily build in your system until your lips hum. An herbal tea slushie refreshes even when mixed with a shot of infused Scotch. Close the meal with longan sticky rice speckled with perilla seeds, showered with crispy coconut and bathed in salted coconut milk that balances the sweetness of the pale lychee fruit and tangy mango ice cream on top. Each bite or sip at OK Chicken is surprising and pleasurable in equal measure. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

In kitchens across the country, chefs have been happily marrying Japanese and Mexican foodways: Both cuisines have a reverence for local grains, honor highly specific seafood preparations, and play on savory, acidic flavors. Ramen Del Barrio blossomed from this shared cultural language — a Japanese Mexican izakaya centering ramen.

Chef and owner Chris Krinsky deftly laces together these threads for dishes such as creamy carnitas tonkotsu with two types of pork, confit buche and belly, as well as a chewy tangle of fresh noodles — made in partnership with Austin chef Gary Wu — using flour from a local mill. A honeycomb tripe and hominy-studded pozole tonkotsu comes rojo- or verde-style, while the mole tsukemen gets paired with thick whole wheat noodles and carnitas for dipping into rich, hearty mole. Tuna tostada, served on top of a sheet of origami paper, packs a zesty punch thanks to a dried shrimp and morita chile aioli, chicharrones furikake, eel sauce, and salsa macha. The yaki-tacos — hefty yakitori skewers served on top of corn tortillas — use smoky pulpo and vegetarian-friendly mushrooms accented with pepitas.

This isn’t fusion for fusion’s sake. Krinsky was born in Maine, grew up in Mexico, and worked at Japanese restaurants throughout most of his career. He started his ramen journey cooking out of his garage and then opened a food court stand, for which he won an Eater Award in 2023. Somehow, his menu tastes better now that he has his own dedicated space where he hand-layered wood panels along the wall and lined the ceiling with sushi mats. A small television in the dining room blasts Spanish-dubbed anime. Ramen Del Barrio 2.0 feels wholly like a loving expression of his culinary fascinations and his commitment to honoring both traditions. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

In an unmarked space in San Francisco’s Nob Hill, chef Patrick Gabon and partner Celine Wuu quietly rewrote the playbook on fine dining with Restaurant Naides. Filipino food has not historically held a footing in the Bay Area’s higher-end echelons, but Naides’s dishes make a powerful claim that the cuisine deserves its place there. Gabon deploys the sour, salty, and sweet flavors of the Philippines with subtle tenacity: The saline funk of bagoong, or fermented salted shrimp, takes on new dimension in Gabon’s hands, where the condiment gets mellowed into a creamy sauce that acts as foil to tender slices of chayote, crisp duck cracklings, and the burst of caviar. His approach to the mouth-puckering sourness of sinigang invigorates the Philippines’ national dish by pouring dry-aged beef broth over meticulously sliced abalone and scallions. These plates manage to retain the soul of the food but in new forms; they don’t placate the audience, asking them instead to reconsider their fundamental notions of fine dining and how Filipino food presented in this way may upend them.

Wuu’s beverage program has become a force of its own. It’s not often that a nonalcoholic pairing manages to outshine a traditional wine program, but Wuu keenly matches the bold flavors of each dish. A drink mixing the flavors of green mango with rooibos and habañero cordial complements the salty punch of bagoong at one turn, while coconut water, osmanthus, and rose vinegar offer a gentle start with the opening snacks, composed of Gabon’s takes on lumpia, okoy, and puto. “As you age and you grow, you tend to go deeper in your roots: ‘How can I make something so traditional the best it can be?’” Wuu told me earlier this year. Naides has answered that question with every meal since. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

It’s tricky to pin down what exactly Rougarou is. It’s a restaurant, certainly, serving modern Southern food in the historic Five Points neighborhood in Denver. It also has a ripping bar program, late-night hours, live music on the patio, and a casual roguish charm. Inside an understated brick building on a flyby street, the dining room is full of personality, dim and moody, all hard surfaces that bounce around the fun clatter of spirited groups throughout the dinner hour.

The menu conveys the right balance of accessibility and intrigue: The ubiquitous tomato stone fruit salad gets a curry-inflected jolt of vinaigrette and a crunch of coconut benne granola. Charred zucchini is doused in smoked cheddar sauce and scattered with bits of country ham. Fried catfish sits on a pond of fermented hot and sour sauce, with pickled chiles that lash the tongue at first and Sichuan peppercorns that leave you gently tingling. And the signature Chicken on a Stick is a lovingly updated homage to a legendary gas station restaurant in Oxford, Mississippi.

While the food feels approachable, the cocktails are high-concept and assertive, leaning on tropical ingredients but pushing for wilder edges, like green banana, oversteeped oolong, and Haitian clairin, pungent and unctuous with fusel oils. A second visit, late at night, revealed a laid-back restaurant-industry hangout at the bar instead of the celebratory din I found earlier. Much like its namesake monster, Rougarou can shape-shift to host a group dinner, a date night, a jam session, or a beguiling nightcap. It’s the kind of restaurant that invites returns, and a great fit for this moment in restaurant culture. — Ben Mesirow, travel editor

D.C. hospitality veterans Jon Sybert and Jill Tyler took a risk when they converted Adams Morgan’s Michelin-starred favorite Tail Up Goat into Rye Bunny, a restaurant that straddles the line between upscale and casual. Appetizers start at $15 and entree prices go up to $40, and instead of table service, diners line up to order at a counter. In the end, both the owners and D.C. diners have seen a payoff. Sybert’s dishes are inventive yet comforting, with Aleppo honey-covered fried chicken served alongside delicately stacked anchovy and quince jam toasts built on thin slices of milk bread. Everything is still seasonal and sourced from nearby farms, but those high-grade ingredients are easier to afford now that the restaurant has been able to cut down on the number of staff by 20 percent. While D.C. diners are not crazy about queuing, the nightly line out the door has sustained for more than six months and become an unexpected way to meet neighbors. A server brings over a drink menu as you wait, so you can catch up with friends and sip on a Slovenian orange wine before you sit down.

Rye Bunny encompasses the simple joy of a neighborhood restaurant that’s an equally excellent destination for a weekday date night or a special occasion, and it represents a larger shift in our dining landscape that might save these mid-price-range restaurants as margins get thinner. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

When So. Fox opened in Atlanta’s Virginia-Highland neighborhood in July, chef Myles Moody and sommelier Rachael Pack had an instant hit, bringing new energy to that pocket of the city. But a successful restaurant often belies monumental effort behind the scenes. So. Fox’s signature dish — a whole roasted chicken — is only available to five lucky tables per night and regularly sells out before the second seating. Much like a great restaurant takes time to build, the simple bird takes days for its mustard brine to infuse, and the result is stunning: a glistening interior and exquisitely crispy skin.

So. Fox commands an insatiable demand for a table topped with that prized poultry, herby rabbit dumplings, and Carolina Gold rice. Snagging a spot at the welcoming bar or at the curved, floating table near the entry, which helps capture overflow crowds, is equally competitive. The space that formerly housed a burger joint (and before that, an auto repair shop) has been transformed into a bright, perennially packed dining room with grand windows, offering an optimal view of North Highland Avenue.

Short for Southern Fox, an American indigenous grape varietal, So. Fox showcases Pack’s longtime knowledge of natural, low-intervention, biodynamic, and Old World producers, many of whom she knows personally. Pack and Atlanta-born Moody first met while working at New York’s Michelin-starred Aska, and returned south to open Kinship Butcher & Sundry in 2021, which resides next door. This isn’t just farm-to-table; it’s produce from their own Ormewood Park farm, highlighted in grilled beef with Vidalia onions and braised leeks, and at the end of summer, in sugar snap peas with chives and farmer cheese.

It’s seasonal Southern fare that feels current and relevant, with a refreshingly casual approach — and people can’t help but show up for it. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater LA

Somssi, from Ahris Kim and chef Daniel Gronert, is one of the clearest examples in New York of a restaurant that goes all-in on personal history, rather than focusing on the broader food culture of any one country or a region.

Korea-born Kim, who ran operations at Atomix, lived in Indonesia and the Philippines before moving to Wisconsin with her family. Gronert, who has German roots and spent time as a pitmaster in South Carolina, cooked across restaurants in Atomix’s parent company. Those influences show up in dishes like the caviar-crowned Potato Potato Potato, a crispy-soft tater tot simulacrum nested on miso hollandaise; ox tongue grilled and glazed with tare, a kaleidoscope of textures; and pork schnitzel presented like shrimp toast (it works).

With the team’s fine dining pedigree, Somssi sets a high bar for hospitality, yet it’s still casual: The room is designed to feel like a home, and the menu nods to places Kim and Gronert have lived.

The bar extends that expertise. Christian Gray’s cocktails include well-made minis, which the bartenders are game to explain to curious drinkers. Sommelier (and Punch contributor) Jenny Eagleton’s list of wines and sakes leans toward lesser-known areas. The duo and their staff reward handing your night over to them, whether you’re there with a group or alone with a Kindle.

Personal touches carry through the space in gloriously analog fashion. Lace curtains on the door spell out the restaurant’s name in embroidery, and handprints line the bathroom wall, left by the broader constellation of people who helped build Somssi into the singular restaurant it is today. — NC

Sunday is a very good night to be at Titusz. That’s Schnitzel Sonntag — when the Pittsburgh restaurant, clad in warm wood and gem-toned ceramic tile, offers an irresistible special at an even more irresistible price: a 4-ounce veal cutlet, breaded and fried in lard, for $13. The golden brown slab comes with a single lemon cheek on the plate and nothing else. It takes confidence to serve a dish so simply: Chef and owner Csilla Thackray gained hers in some of the city’s top restaurant kitchens. She named Titusz after her great-grandfather, and his portrait hangs by the first-floor bar. Her own name comes from her Budapest-born grandmother, who raised the chef on her cooking.

Call it grandmacore if you want to peg Titusz to a national trend, but the menu is modern, Austrian, Hungarian, and distinctly Thackray’s. Here, meggyleves, the Magyar sour-cherry soup, gets an electrifying swirl of paprika oil. The chef has made charring an art: You will want to pick up the bowl and drink every drop of charred leek and sauerkraut broth beneath her buoyant kaspressknödel (cheese dumplings). The Maillard reaction pays off again in the savory brown butter drizzled over a dessert of aranygaluska (think walnut monkey bread), served warm on a puddle of peach creme anglaise. Thackray’s husband — Sean Rosenkrans, another veteran of Pittsburgh’s restaurant scene — has built a stunning list of wines from Central Europe, as well as cocktails fluent in that idiom — a slug of herbal Unicum here, a toasty hint of caraway there. Everything makes profound and reassuring sense together. The decision to spend money at a restaurant might feel fraught right now; the choices at Titusz never do. — Beth Kracklauer, dining editorial manager

#6433. Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip

From a naked eye perspective, stars are stable and predictable. Not much goes on but shining. The Sun itself is fairly plane and nondescript and will shine relatively steadily for billions of years. It's considered a low-mass star compared to the most massive stars, which are rarer and contain many times its mass.

Powerful telescopes bring millions of stars of different types and ages into view. Astrophysicists and astronomers watch the Sun and its low-mass brethren, and note changes in their shining, just as they do all types of stars. Their observations reveal the changes stars experience during their long lifetimes.

As low-mass stars like the Sun exhaust their hydrogen supplies and evolve, they become Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars. This is not only theoretical, it's an observational conclusion. RGB stars are easy to observe and study for two reasons: they're bright, and they're numerous. Arcturus, Aldebaran, and Pollus are all bright, naked-eye stars and are all RGB stars. (Well-known Betelgeuse is a Red Supergiant, not quite the same.)

As RGB stars age and cool, they swell in size and become more luminous. It's a pretty steady change. But for some reason, there's a brief and abrupt dip in their brightness known as the RGB luminosity bump. The bump is called that because of how it appears in the colourâmagnitude diagrams of stellar clusters.

Astrophysicists know why the bump ends. But what initiates the bump is still unexplained. Astrophysicists don't like this gap in their knowledge and they've been trying to fill it in.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters has an explanation for the bump. It's titled "The Role of Specific Entropy in the Onset of the Luminosity Bump," and the sole author is Saskia Hekker. Hekker is a Professor of Theoretical Astrophysics and the Group Leader of the Theory and Observations of Stars Group at the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies.

"During their evolution, stars follow a distinct path in luminosityâtemperature space. Low-mass stars that have exhausted hydrogen in their core follow the so-called red-giant branch (RGB), which is predominantly in the direction of increasing luminosity and decreasing surface temperature," Hekker explains. "The luminosity bump is a temporary decrease in luminosity against this otherwise increasing trend."

The inset grey box is the Hertzsprung-Russel diagram for a 1 solar mass star progressing from the subgiant branch to the tip of the Red Giant Branch. The tiny grey box inside it is magnified in the larger part of the image, highlighting the RGB luminosity bump. Image Credit: S. Hekker 2026 ApJL 1008 L61

The bump is understood theoretically and also confirmed with observations. But there's one discrepancy between theory and observation. In models, the bump appears at higher luminosities than the observed bump, meaning it appears later. "To understand why the bump appears later in the models than in observations, the physics of the bump needs to be unravelled," Hekker writes.

Stars, including our Sun, are layered, and RGB stars are no exception. But unlike the Sun, RGB stars have exhausted the hydrogen in their cores, and most of what's left is in their envelopes. Since the core has exhausted its hydrogen by fusing it into helium, the core is inert helium. An RGB's fusion occurs in a thin shell. In both these regions, energy is transported via radiation.

Above this radiative region is a convective outer envelope.

As an RGB star ascends the branch, the core contracts and the surface expands. Since the core is inert helium, it exerts no outward pressure and is forced inward. "This causes the deepest layer of the convective envelope to move inwards, reaching layers that have changed their chemical composition due to (burning) processes earlier in the evolution of the star," Hekker explains.

This is when dredge-up occurs, as deeper layers are forced into the convective zone. Since the convective zone is convective, the material from the radiative zone mixes into the convective zone, changing its composition.

Now there's a situation where there's a shifting boundary deep inside the star called the Base of the Convective Zone (BCZ). It's organized around a thermodynamic property called specific entropy. It basically measures how disordered the gas is at the BCZ. As the BCZ moves deeper inside the star, the entropy difference across the boundary shrinks. Past a certain point, entropy across the boundary layer drops past a critical value, and that triggers the luminosity bump.

This diagram shows the interior of an RGB star (not to scale). An inert helium core is in the center, and it's contained in a thin hydrogen-burning shell. Above that is a radiative zone separated from the star's convective envelope by the base of the convective zone (BCZ). Earlier dredge-up and mixing created this boundary between helium-enriched and hydrogen-rich gas. This work ties the RGB luminosity bump to this boundary. The author argues that the onset of the bump occurs when the entropy across this boundary crosses a critical value. (Image Generated with AI)

Previous explanations for the bump rested on mechanics. In those explanations, the thin hydrogen-burning shell reaches the boundary and something inside the star changes, triggering the bump. In this explanation, the bump happens when an entropy threshold is crossed inside the star's thermodynamics. It's not simply that layers meet.

We can't see inside stars. Astrophysicists use physics to try to understand what's going on there, and they test those physics against the only part of the star they can really see, the outside. It's a constant back and forth to refine theories until they match observations.

âThis succinct explanation of the onset of the bump, is the first quantitative description proposed so far,â said Hekker.

This new work will make its way into the larger body of astrophysical theory.

"This viable description of the mechanism behind the onset of the bump provides crucial and new insights for the exploitation of the bump as an anchor point in stellar evolution theory," Hekker writes. "Such added knowledge of the onset of the bump could potentially be used to make more informed choices for changes to the physics in stellar models that go beyond calibration of the overshoot, to place the bump in stellar evolution models at the correct luminosity while at the same time aligning them with measured surface abundances."

A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.

This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.

"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."

In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.

The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.

"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."

Archaeologists found a chair made from the trunk of an alder tree near the man's burial. The chair was likely a symbol of authority or power.

To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."

The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.

But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.

"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."

While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.

Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Myburgh, D. A., da Silva, N. A., Romeyer-Dherbey, J. H., Grefen-Peters, S., Jöns, H., Peek, C., Nebel, A., & Krause-Kyora, B. (2026). Paleogenomics reveals leprosy at the late antique burial site of Fallward in northern Germany. iScience, 29(11), 117877. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117877

What do you know about the bones in your body? Test your knowledge with our human skeleton quiz.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6430. First Direct Measurement of Cosmic Hydrogen Could Change How We Map the Universe

Advances in computing and astronomy have led to increasingly complex attempts to chart the large-scale structure of the Universe. For the past decade, scientists have been working to map one aspect in particular to see whether it matches observations of the cosmic web: cosmic hydrogen. For the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang, neutral hydrogen was the only element in the Universe (known as the "Cosmic Dark Ages") and provided the feedstock for stars, galaxies, and the cosmic web.

Today, it remains the most abundant element in the Universe and can be found everywhere - the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM) - in abundance. For the past decade, scientists with the MeerKLASS Collaboration have been trying to measure how neutral hydrogen "clumps" in the distant Universe. In a study published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), the team announced the first direct measurement of the large-scale structure of cosmic hydrogen.

The MeerKLASS (MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey) Collaboration is an international group of astronomers conducting cosmological surveys using the MeerKAT radio telescope. Their survey relies on a technique known as HI intensity (or 21-cm intensity) mapping to detect the combined emissions of galaxies within large segments of the sky. This enables the creation of 3D maps of the cosmos that show the distribution of matter (gas, dust, stars, galaxies, clusters, etc.) in the cosmic web.

Members of the MeerKLASS collaboration at their biannual 'Busy Week' meeting, hosted at the University of Torino in September 2025. Credit: SARAO

This is no easy task, since the 21-cm signal must be extracted from all the other emissions of the Universe (the "foreground noise"), which are about 10,000 times stronger than the hydrogen signal itself. To accomplish this, the team chose to operate each dish in the array as an independent telescope, rather than combining all 64 dishes into a single interferometer. This was an entirely new observation mode for MeerKAT that traded sharp angular resolution for very high survey speed.

For their survey, the team analyzed data collected by the MeerKAT array across ~250 square degrees of sky. This enabled the detection of a neutral hydrogen signal that originated 4.5 billion years ago (or 9 billion years after the Big Bang). The team's measurements produced many independent maps from different dishes and observing times. These were then cross-compared to suppress individual instrument effects and reinforce the structure of cosmic hydrogen.

Their results showed that cosmic hydrogen mirrors the large-scale structure of the cosmic web, advancing a technique that could transform how cosmologists map the Universe. Dr Steven Cunnington, a Senior Research Fellow at Purdue University's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, led the development of the analysis pipeline that enabled the mapping of cosmic hydrogen. Since 2015, he has also co-led one of the working groups within the MeerKLASS Collaboration.

As he expressed in a University of Portsmouth release:

This result feels particularly special because it's the culmination of a journey that began when I started my PhD at Portsmouth over a decade ago. I am now fortunate to be part of a much wider international collaboration sharing this common goal. Many of the challenges addressed in this work have shaped my own research career, so seeing our team deliver this measurement is a remarkable milestone to witness.

This slice of the DESI data maps celestial objects from Earth (center) to billions of light-years away, showing nearby bright galaxies (yellow), luminous red galaxies (orange), emission-line galaxies (blue), and quasars (green). Credit: DESI Collaboration/DOE/KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/C. Lamman

This information can be used to constrain the most pressing cosmological measurements facing scientists today. This includes the expansion rate of the cosmos (the Hubble-LemaÃ®tre Constant), the influence of Dark Energy, and the distribution of Dark Matter. Said Professor MÃ¡rio Santos, Principal Investigator of the MeerKLASS survey at the University of the Western Cape:

This is a milestone in establishing 21-cm intensity mapping as a novel tool for cosmology. This measurement took a decade of patient work by researchers spread across seven countries and three continents - and many of them are early-career scientists who have spent their whole career on this project. Such an ambitious result requires sustained and genuine teamwork from many people. And none of it would exist without the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, which built and operates MeerKAT and helped sort out the many challenges with this survey along the way. It is a reminder that science at this level is a large collaborative effort.

#6428. ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar

There's a strange gamma-ray emitter in the Large Magellanic Cloud that has astronomers stumped about its source. It lies within the ashes left behind by a supernova that created a compact object that's part of the system. The supernova remnant provides a piece of evidence to explain the emissions, but not the whole story.

So, a research team from two Japanese universities decided to give the object, called LMC P3, a closer look. Instead of tracking the gamma rays, they looked at the object with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile. This is a series of radio telescopes that provide highly detailed radio views of objects in the sky. ALMA focused on radio emissions from carbon monoxide (CO) molecules in proximity to the cold cloud in the area around LMC P3. It's one of the few such objects found outside the Milky Way, and astronomers have dubbed it a microquasar. It consists of a giant O-type star and a compact object that could be explained by the existence of a black hole or a neutron star.

According to astronomer Yasuo Fukui of Nagoya University, who worked with team leader Bhuvana Gadikere Rajendra of Gifu University, what they detected at LMC P3 is unusual. âWe discovered a gigantic molecular jet,â said Fukui. The jet consists of molecular gas that stretches out across 26 light-years of space. For reference, the bright star Vega lies 25 light-years away from us, so the jet would connect us and that star quite easily.

The strange thing is, the molecular jet itself is cold (by our standards), but astrophysically "heated" to a temperature of about 35 to 60 Kelvin. By comparison, that's warmer than the 15 Kelvin surrounding gas but still very cold. That temperature difference means that the gas is interacting with another jet— this one a high-energy stream of particles coming from the nearby compact object with enough energy to power gamma-ray emissions. The object turns out to be a micro-quasar, which would have the energy to do the job.

Micro-quasars are interesting objects. They actually consist of two objects: a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star coupled with a companion star. The black hole constantly sucks material from the star, and that creates a swirling accretion disk around the black hole. It's a fairly energetic interaction that leads to X-ray and gamma-ray emissions. It also creates high-speed jets that travel out at nearly light-speed velocities. They're called micro-quasars because they're a smaller type of quasar, which is a highly active region around a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy.

Fukui said the relatively high temperature observed over a large fraction of the molecular cloud makes it a very strong case that the gas is interacting with a high-energy jet coming from the compact object â precisely the kind of jet that can also power LMC P3âs gamma rays. This also provides a boost to the idea that the object is a black hole, leftover from the collapse of a supermassive star in a supernova explosion.

Prior to this discovery, scientists had two competing theories about what could be powering the emissions. One is that pulsar winds could have been causing the emissions. That means the object has to be a pulsar, which would send out streams of energetic particles in pulsations as the object spins. Neutron stars are created when a supermassive star collapses, but a stellar remnant remains behind consisting solely of neutrons packed tightly together in a space about the size of a city.

The other theory is that the object is indeed a microquasar. The discovery of the newly found "cold" jet strongly suggests that the compact object could be a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star that draws in material from its companion to form an accretion disk. Since black holes drive more powerful jets than neutron stars, the fact that LMC P3âs gamma-ray emission is particularly high is a smoking gun pointing toward the micro-quasar origin of the signals found by ALMA. âIt provides very strong support for the possibility that its central object is a black hole," said Fukui.

Object LMC P3 was first discovered in 2016 thanks to its very strong gamma-ray emissions. It was also the first one found outside the Milky Way. From the beginning, astronomers suspected it was an X-ray binary, and Chandra X-ray Observatory studies seemed to confirm that. Then, the FERMI telescope observed it and found a 10.3-day period in gamma-ray emissions from the object. That suggested a number of ideas, including jets.

Detailed observations with ALMA focused on the surrounding gas clouds and found the "cold" jet streaming away. That raised questions about the "launch mechanism" for such a jet. In the paper the team published about their observations, they wrote: "We interpret that the high temperatures are due to shock heating of a microquasar jet driven by the gamma-ray binary, where the compact object has an accretion disk fed by the O-star winds. The CO jet matches existing predictions from magnetohydrodynamical simulations, which show that a CO jet can form from the interaction of the microquasar jet and an ambient interstellar medium (ISM) cloud. These results provide strong evidence that CO jets are a signature sculpted by microquasar jets, lending support for mass accretion in LMC P3 as the gamma-ray origin.

This discovery has important astrophysical implications for the study of high-energy emissions and the objects that provide them. Coupled with ongoing studies of such objects as SS 433, which is the first microquasar ever found, discoveries such as LMC P3 give new insight into the actions of compact objects and their interactions with surrounding objects.

Has a Mysterious Gamma-ray Powerhouse Revealed its Smoking Gun?

#6427. Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way

If we want big things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

Telescopes like the JWST feature ingenious folding designs that unfold in space like insects metamorphosizing. That was a very impressive way to bypass the restrictions imposed by rocket fairings. But that's not practical in every case.

What's far more feasible is sending smaller components into space inside fairings and then assembling them into a larger structure once there. That's what NOM4D, the Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design program is demonstrating. NOM4D reached an important milestone recently when it successfully demonstrated automated in-space assembly for the first time.

The demonstration involved a gantry robot, also known as a linear robot, building a typical truss structure. Gantry robots move in straight lines along x, y, and z axes. The payload came from Caltech and consisted of individual components with custom joints put together to form the structure. The individual components were not only assembled, but a thin reflective mesh that mimics what a space-based antenna might have was also simultaneously applied.

âNOM4Dâs objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space,â said Andrew Detor, NOM4D program manager. âBy âvery large,â I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.â

This concept image shows a space-based antenna autonomously assembled by a NOM4D-type device. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

There is no shortage of ideas of how space-based manufacturing and construction could be used, but it all starts with programs like NOM4D. NOM4D is fairly simple at this point, like a child's construction toy, but that's its strength.

âYou can think of the Caltech approach as similar to Tinkertoys or Kânex construction toys: individual truss members are joined at nodes, one section at a time, to create a larger structure,â Detor said. âWithin the automated assembly box, each section is built piece by piece, a reflective mesh is attached, and the assembled sections are deployed as they are complete. There are no complicated robotics or advanced algorithms; itâs just solid engineering from the Caltech team to combine operations in a way that scales.â

Decades ago, thinkers proposed different types of rotating space stations that could be homes for thousands of people. The O'Neill Cylinder is probably the most well-known one of these, and space-heads and sci-fi dreamers of a certain age may have carried around a dog-eared copy of Gerard K. O'Neill's "The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space."

"More important than material issues, I think there is reason to hope that the opening of a new, high frontier will challenge the best that is in us, that the new lands waiting to be built in space will give us new freedom to search for better governments, social systems, and ways of life, and that our children may thereby find a world richer in opportunity by our efforts during the decades ahead," O'Neill wrote.

The O'Neill Cylinder lies in the realm of science fiction or the distant future for now, as do O'Neill's hopes for humanity. But that was 50 years ago, and technology has advanced considerably, even if how humans conduct themselves hasn't advanced at the same pace.

But there are other proposed space structures that are closer to reality, and they may be stages towards O'Neill's hopeful vision that can be built by NOM4D or its successor.

It may begin with Low-Earth Orbit transfer stations and lunar orbit stations that would expand our presence in space. The proposed Lunar Gateway was one of these, and was envisioned as a modular design built in space from pre-made components. It would be a docking station and communications relay facility for trips to the lunar surface and operations there. These types of orbital facilities could be hybrids of pre-made components and structural frameworks made by NOM4D or something like it.

This concept image shows how a NOM4D-inspired device might autonomously construct a circular truss structure in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

Another future use for scalable construction concerns lunar lava tubes. The Moon has what appear to be networks of subsurface lava tubes that provide natural protection from hazards. Robotic assembly could feasibly be used to reinforce these natural tubes and turn them into habitats.

Another idea is liquid mirror telescopes. Building a huge telescope mirror and sending it into space would be near impossible, but a liquid mirror telescope could be built in a lunar crater out of components shipped individually into space. And NASA's Lunar Crater Radio Telescope (LCRT) is a concept for a crater-based telescope on the lunar far side, isolated from Earth's radio pollution. These ideas are waiting for the engineering to catch up.

âIn a future space economy, weâre going to need large things,â Detor said. âThink large space depots or habitats, large solar arrays to collect power, or large radio antennas to explore the edges of the universe. Those things require size, and NOM4D gives us a path to accelerate creation of new capabilities.â

The rapid advancement of the NOM4D program surprised even NOM4D personnel themselves. This successful on-orbit demonstration wasn't expected to happen so soon.

Back in February 2025, NOM4D changed its timeline. What was expected to be a third phase of more laboratory tests was instead changed to on-orbit tests, and SpaceX launched Caltech's NOM4D payload into space in March 2026.

âCaltech [California Institute of Technology] and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have demonstrated tremendous advances in the first two phases and have now partnered in Phase 3 with space-launch companies to conduct in-space testing of their novel assembly processes and materials,â Detor said at the time. âOriginally, Phase 3 was going to be about making things more precisely in the lab than we did in Phase 2. But we said, âYou know, the maturity is there, and there would be more impact if we took the capabilities we have now and actually go demonstrate them in space to show that it can be done,â"Detor said.

Now, way ahead of its original schedule, NOM4D has demonstrated its capabilities and is maturing rapidly. As Detor makes clear, leaping from the laboratory to space is a huge jump.

âItâs the speed and the scale that made this a DARPA project. We went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype into space in 15 months,â Detor said. âOperating in space is much harder than operating on the ground â thereâs virtually no margin to address issues that may arise. Testing in the operational environment is instrumental to rapidly maturing the technology.â

There's still another test upcoming for NOM4D now that it's demonstrated successful on-orbit assembly. Next, the NOM4D team from University of Illinois Urbana-Champagne will launch a test project to the ISS. This will be more than just assembly; it will demonstrate composite material processing. A monomer resin will be used to build a high-strength structure in space. It will use an energy-efficient method to heat the resin and create a strong polymer. This is similar to how resins are used in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) manufacturing to build things like aerospace components, where strength and light weight are critical.

If that test is successful, then it really will be time to start thinking big, according to Detor.

This concept image shows what the future of NOM4D-like construction might look like. Large space structures like these could be built entirely in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

âThe NOM4D Caltech demonstration is not an endpoint; itâs a beginning,â Detor said. âNow that weâve demonstrated a process that can scale to large structures, what do we go make? What wild ideas get assembled thousands of miles above us and what new capabilities do those structures enable?â

Is it time to open Gerard K. O'Neill's seminal book again?

The O'Neill Cylinder, the OG of space habitats. Maybe one day. Image Credit: By NASA/Rick Guidice - https://space.nss.org/settlement/nasa/70sArtHiRes/70sArt/art.html (image link), Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=675434

Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.

The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.

Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.

Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.

To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"

The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.

A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.

Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.

"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."

Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.

The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

#6424. Iran Is Handing Out Iodine Pills Near Pickaxe Mountain. Here’s What a Nuclear Strike There Would Actually Do.

Whether or not the U.S. ever drops a nuke on the granite complex, the physics of attacking something buried 100 meters underground explains why Tehran is telling people to “get inside, stay inside.”

Since the U.S. and Israel launched a military campaign against Iran on February 28, Washington and Tehran have sparred over whether Pickaxe Mountain (Kūh-e Kolang Gaz Lā) in the Karkas Mountains in central Iran is the secretive site of the country’s nuclear enrichment efforts. In past statements, U.S. President Donald Trump has made vague threats regarding the site, saying that the U.S. would “take care of it.” In September, he added: “We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard.”

What that means is anyone’s guess, but this week political commentator Tucker Carlson wrote on X—without offering evidence—that the U.S. was possibly “within days” of launching a nuclear strike on the site. The White House responded that Carlson has “no insight into military planning,” and Trump himself ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran in mid-October. Still, Trump told reporters Thursday that a decision on renewed strikes is coming “soon,” and the Iranians, at least, are behaving as though they take the nuclear scenario seriously.

That’s the part worth understanding. According to The Times, Iran’s health ministry is distributing iodine tablets to residents within a two-to-three-kilometer radius of nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe. A video circulating on Iranian social media walks viewers through a hypothetical nuclear explosion at the site, listing distances to nearby cities—17 miles to Natanz, 25 to Kashan, 117 to Isfahan, 223 to Tehran—and offering three instructions: “Get inside, stay inside and listen for updates.” It warns that people near the site might have only 10 to 15 minutes to do so. One Iranian analyst told the paper, “If America does not use a nuclear weapon against Pickaxe Mountain, it will be a miracle.”

So what, exactly, are they preparing for?

Potassium iodide doesn’t protect you from radiation in general. It does one narrow job: it saturates the thyroid with stable iodine so the gland can’t absorb radioactive iodine-131, a fission product that concentrates in the thyroid and is a leading cause of post-fallout thyroid cancer, especially in children. I-131 has a half-life of about eight days, which is why the pills are a first-week countermeasure rather than a long-term one. Handing them out is what a government does when its planning assumption is a fission event upwind of populated areas—as opposed to a conventional bombing, which produces no I-131 at all.

Pickaxe first entered the public record in September 2020, two months after an explosion destroyed an above-ground centrifuge-assembly workshop at Natanz. Iran’s then-nuclear chief, Ali Akbar Salehi, said work had begun on a “more modern, larger and more comprehensive” replacement inside a nearby mountain. Satellite imagery since then shows four fortified tunnel portals, internal roads, possible ventilation shafts, and an expanding security perimeter—but International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors have never been inside, and no schematics exist in the public domain. Analysts say the halls could house centrifuge production, an enrichment plant, or protected storage for Iran’s roughly 440 kilograms of 60-percent-enriched uranium. Back in July, The Wall Street Journal reported that Israeli intelligence told the U.S. that Iran had moved centrifuges to the site following the 12-day war that started in June 2025.

Estimates put parts of the complex 80 to 100 meters (roughly 260 to 330 feet) underground, in granite. For comparison, the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—the 30,000-pound bunker buster used for the first time in combat during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025—is generally credited with penetrating around 200 feet of earth, and considerably less through hard rock. At Fordow, the U.S. compensated by dropping six MOPs in sequence down each of two ventilation shafts, each bomb boring deeper than the last. It’s not publicly known whether Pickaxe has comparable shafts to exploit, or how many MOPs remain in the inventory.

“Pickaxe Mountain is a deeply buried granite fortification, and it will be difficult to destroy the facility even with the heaviest nonnuclear U.S. munitions, such as the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator,” the Center for Strategic & International Studies reported in September 2026. “While military strikes may degrade or temporarily disable Pickaxe Mountain, continuously bombing Iranian nuclear infrastructure is unsustainable.”

The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or “Mother of All Bombs,” which CBS News reported is also in Pentagon planning, is a different animal entirely: it works by creating overpressure, not by blasting through rock. It could kill personnel in tunnels open to the air and wreck surface infrastructure, but it’s not a bunker buster.

What a nuclear strike would do—and why that’s the dirty option

The U.S. arsenal holds both strategic nuclear weapons (the ones capable of leveling entire cities) and tactical nuclear weapons, such as the lower-yield B61 family of gravity bombs. Newsweek reports one scenario in which the U.S. would first soften the site with several GBU-57s before following up with a B61. The weapon most often mentioned is the B61-11, the Pentagon’s only dedicated earth-penetrating nuclear bomb, with a reported yield of up to around 400 kilotons—roughly 25 times Hiroshima. The newest variant, the B61-13, pairs the B61-12’s precision-guided tail kit with a yield of up to about 360 kilotons. It’s carried only by strategic bombers like the B-2, entered production in 2025, and was pitched by the Pentagon as an option against “harder and large-area military targets.”

Here’s the catch: None of these bombs goes deep. The B61-11 is designed to punch only a few meters into the ground before detonating, the B61-12 can manage a few meters at most, and the B61-13 would go off at or near the surface, relying on sheer yield. A weapon that goes off even a short distance underground transfers far more of its energy into the rock as a shock wave than an air burst does, which is how it can collapse tunnels a hundred meters down. But a few meters is nowhere near deep enough to contain the explosion. Underground test data suggests that fully containing a blast in the 400-kiloton range would require burying it something like 800 meters deep. No deliverable bomb comes close to that.

So whichever bomb is used, the burst behaves, for fallout purposes, like the worst kind of ground burst. The fireball vaporizes thousands of tons of granite and soil, mixes it with the bomb’s own fission products—iodine-131, cesium-137, strontium-90—and lofts the whole radioactive mess into a plume that drops back to Earth downwind over hours and days. That’s the fallout Iran’s iodine pills are for. The centrifuges and enriched uranium inside would be pulverized and dispersed too, though uranium itself is a comparatively minor radiological hazard; the bomb’s fission debris does the real damage.

Where it lands depends on the weather. Prevailing winds over central Iran run broadly west to east, which would push a plume away from Tehran and toward Yazd, the eastern provinces, and potentially Afghanistan and Pakistan. The heaviest fallout falls within tens of miles, so India Today’s questions about whether detectable radiation could reach South Asia aren’t crazy, though doses that far out would be low. Those “10 to 15 minutes” in the Iranian video are about the lethal early fallout close in, which is why the advice is to get indoors immediately rather than to flee.

If a strike happens over the weekend, confirmation won’t depend on anyone’s press release. Seismometers around the world would register the event within minutes, and a nuclear explosion looks different from an earthquake or a string of conventional bombs: it causes a sharp, compressional first motion rather than the shearing signature of a fault slipping. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization operates a global network of seismic, infrasound, and radionuclide stations that routinely catches North Korean tests; its air samplers would pick up radioactive xenon isotopes—which nothing but fission produces—within a day or two. A MOP strike, by contrast, would show up as small, repeated surface-coupled thumps with no xenon.

For all the attention Carlson’s post has drawn, most experts expect a nuclear option to remain a remote possibility.

“I don’t think it’s very likely—as rash as President Trump is, I think he knows what would be the great implications of that,” Yale University’s Arash Azizi, a Middle East analyst, told DW News. “I should say though that I’ve heard the same from Iranian officials in the last few months. It is a worry that they have that he will cross that line that has of course never been crossed since 1945.”

Other experts speaking with Newsweek were blunter, calling such an attack “catastrophically stupid”—not primarily because of the fallout, but because of what it would signal. The first use of a nuclear weapon since 1945, against a non-nuclear state, would, in their assessment, undercut the Non-Proliferation Treaty and give other governments a vivid reason to conclude that only a deterrent of their own keeps them safe.

The realistic range of outcomes, then, runs from a negotiated pause—Qatari mediators were still working the phones Thursday—to a conventional strike package built around MOPs, cruise missiles against the portals and ventilation shafts, and possibly a MOAB. Even that leaves open the question CSIS raised: a facility 100 meters down in granite can be sealed, cut off, and set back, but “destroyed” is a harder word to earn. Fordow was declared “obliterated” in June 2025, and the argument over what that meant hasn’t ended. Pickaxe is deeper underground, so the likelihood of it surviving a nonnuclear strike is higher.

For now, a nuclear strike remains only a hypothetical scenario. But Iranian officials are reportedly handing out iodine pills and telling people how far they live from a mountain. That tells you what they’re planning for—and the physics of bunker-busting explains why.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.

Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.

Archaeologists found evidence of cannabis use in a burial mound in southern Siberia.

Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.

But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

Caspari, G., Sadykov, T., Formicheva, D., Blochin, J., Armbruster, D., Happel, O., Ryabogina, N., Boxleitner, K., Spengler, R. (2026). Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago. Science. http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800
