#6389. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

#6387. Simple fungi can recognize shapes, like circles and crosses, when looking for wood to eat

Scientists found that a brainless wood-rotting fungus can recognize shapes. It grows differently on circles versus crosses, suggesting these simple organisms can process spatial patterns.

A fungus has no brain, no eyes, and no nerves. Yet a wood-rotting fungus, given a cross of wood blocks to grow on, attached more of its threads to the outer blocks than to the inner ones.

Given a circle to grow on, it showed no such pattern and left the center bare. The researchers suggested the difference may be a form of pattern recognition.

Yu Fukasawa of Tohoku University in Japan led the 2024 study with colleagues at Tohoku and at Nagaoka College.

The fungus they used lives on forest floors and builds its networks by sending thick strands of thread, called cords, from one piece of dead wood to the next.

Its name is Phanerochaete velutina, and Fukasawa’s team had earlier found that it remembers the direction to a piece of wood.

“You’d be surprised at just how much fungi are capable of,” Fukasawa said. “They have memories, they learn, and they can make decisions. Quite frankly, the differences in how they solve problems compared to humans is mind-blowing.”

Even so, the team phrased its own conclusion as a question, not a verdict.

The mushroom in the video above is a pink oyster, not the fungus in this study. Pink oysters, named for their salmon-pink caps, grow on dead hardwood and are farmed on straw as food.

The study’s fungus grows as a thin crust on wood, with no cap or stem. Both break down dead wood with a network of threads.

Fukasawa’s team cut beech wood into cubes less than half an inch (1 cm) on a side, weighed them, and let the fungus grow into them for six weeks.

The team then set nine cubes on each tray of damp soil, in a circle or in a cross, with 2 inches (5 cm) between neighboring blocks. Each tray was about 9.5 inches (24 cm) square, and there were ten of each shape.

Everything but the shape was the same from tray to tray. The trays stayed in the dark at 68°F (20°C) for 116 days, nearly four months.

Once a week the team misted them with sterile water and moved them around the incubator. A camera 18 inches (46 cm) above the trays photographed each one monthly.

At the end, the researchers counted the cords attached to each block, then dried and weighed the blocks again to see how much wood the fungus had broken down.

After 116 days, cords ran from block to block across every tray, though a few blocks ended up with no cord attached at all.

In the cross, the four blocks at the ends of the arms had more cords than the four middle blocks and the one at the center. The count ran from zero cords on some blocks to nine on others.

In the circle, no position in the ring had reliably more cords than another. The cross result was the opposite of what the team had predicted.

They had expected the center block, the one with four neighbors, to be the most connected, and instead the blocks at the ends of the arms were.

The team suggested the outer blocks may have worked as outposts, where the fungus absorbed water and nutrients from the soil. The inner blocks, with fewer cords, may have become little more than a path for cords passing through.

The more cords a block had, the more of its wood the fungus had broken down. Blocks in the circle lost between 18% and 65.5% of their dry weight, and blocks in the cross lost between 16.7% and 62.7%. Overall, the cross blocks lost a little less than the circle blocks did.

The researchers also reran the analysis without the extreme blocks, the ones with no cords or with nine. Without them, the difference between the two shapes faded, while the link between cords and decay remained.

The fungus also spread roughly the same amount of thread over the soil in both shapes. So the cross blocks didn’t decay less because the fungus grew less. The network was built differently, and the wood decayed differently.

The recognition argument rests on that difference. In a human brain, different images activate different groups of neurons, and that contrast in activity is what lets the brain recognize an image.

A network of fungal threads that builds itself one way for a cross and another for a circle may be doing something similar, Fukasawa’s team wrote.

Every block started the same way, with threads growing outward in all directions. Then the fronts from neighboring blocks met and fused into one body.

In the circle trays, the merged fungus kept growing outward, and by day 34 a large bare patch had formed at the center.

Fukasawa’s team compared this to fairy rings, the circles of mushrooms that widen year after year because the fungus beneath them grows outward from its edge. Why the fused network left the center empty is something the team can’t yet explain.

One possibility they raised is crowding: fungal growth is known to stop once the threads get dense enough, and the threads inside the ring may have reached that point.

Whether the fungus is conscious is irrelevant, the team wrote, because cognition can run without consciousness even in a brain.

Slime molds, which also have no brain, have already solved a maze and linked food sources with networks about as efficient as a real railway.

The team raised one possible explanation, and it involves rhythm. The amount of calcium at each growing tip rises and falls in a cycle, and so do the flow of material and the electrical activity through the fungus.

When separate colonies fuse, those rhythms tend to synchronize, and synchronized rhythms may be how the network carries information about where things are.

The rhythm idea is a hypothesis, and this experiment didn’t measure it. The team also can’t yet say whether the tray lids affected the empty center of the ring.

The lids were loose and came off every week, so the researchers doubt the middle ran short of oxygen. The way to settle it is a tray with no lid, and that’s the experiment they said would be worth running.

The full study was published in the journal Fungal Ecology.

#6386. The Grand Canyon’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to over six miles of hidden caves

Researchers mapped over six miles of caves beneath the Grand Canyon, revealing how groundwater flows and why its drinking water faces pollution risks.

For decades, the twelve different water spigots used by visitors in Grand Canyon National Park have drawn their water from Roaring Springs, a cave-fed spring on the North Rim.

In an August 2025 study, researchers at Northern Arizona University (NAU) described over 6 miles (10 kilometers) of cave passages behind the spring. They mapped them with a handheld lidar scanner.

The 3D maps reveal the passages that carry water through the limestone below the North Rim. That system is fast and vulnerable to contamination from the surface.

The park’s water supply has served more than 6 million visitors a year from that single cave spring. Its water is almost entirely snowmelt from the Kaibab Plateau.

Built starting in 1965, the 12½-mile (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline carried that water toward the South Rim and its 800-plus historic buildings.

The aging pipe had at least 85 major breaks between 2010 and mid-2026, according to the National Park Service. A single break often tops $25,000 to repair.

A replacement project shifts the South Rim intake to Bright Angel Creek near Phantom Ranch. On August 29, 2026, a flash flood destroyed a water intake pump and other infrastructure.

The Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs intake areas “sustained significant damage,” the park reported in a September 2026 update. Roughly 40 percent of the old pipeline between Phantom Ranch and the North Rim was also damaged.

The South Rim has been under Stage 4 water restrictions while the park arranged to truck in about 200,000 gallons (757,000 liters) a day. Pumping from Bright Angel Creek to a new treatment plant could begin by November 16.

Blase LaSala, a Ph.D. student in ecoinformatics at NAU’s School of Informatics, Computing, and Cyber Systems, led the mapping. He worked with NAU professor Temuulen “Teki” Sankey, a remote sensing expert.

With park staff and volunteers, the team scanned Roaring Springs Cave, Muav West Cave and Redwall East Cave. The handheld scanner uses near-infrared laser light and records up to 300,000 points per second.

The crews documented more than 6.3 miles (10.2 kilometers) of passages in 25 days. The caves extend beyond 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) from their entrances and 1,300 feet (400 meters) below them.

In Muav West Cave, the lidar maps agreed 98 percent with a traditional survey, which covered about half the distance in the same time.

“I had no idea how large and long these caves are,” Sankey said. “Grand Canyon’s caves have never been mapped in 3D like this.”

Karst forms where water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone, opening caves, conduits and sinkholes.

The caves lie in the Redwall and Muav limestones, karst layers some 2,300 feet (700 meters) beneath the plateau surface. Water travels through these limestone layers via steep fractures and underground conduits.

Abe Springer, an NAU professor and co-author, also worked with the park on dye tracing tests. Dye dropped into surface sinkholes reached springs about 12 miles (20 kilometers) away in as little as a week.

From the 3D models, the authors conclude that today’s groundwater follows near-vertical cracks and the tilt of the rock layers. They link those patterns to regional faulting and uplift.

In Redwall East Cave, bubble trails and other features sit above the stream passage. They suggest that today’s flow may reuse pathways carved by an older aquifer.

“It’s like looking at a black box,” LaSala explained. “You see what comes in and what comes out, but it’s very hard to quantify what’s going on in there.”

The researchers describe karst aquifers like this one as both vulnerable to contamination and challenging to model.

Runoff from burned areas or E. coli bacteria entering sinkholes linked to Roaring Springs Cave could force the park to halt its pumps, NAU warns.

The Dragon Bravo Fire, which started on July 4, 2025, burned 149,399 acres (60,460 hectares), including 71,129 acres (28,785 hectares) of the park.

The park’s burned area emergency response listed protection of the drinking water system among its treatments.

The fire also changed conditions on the Kaibab Plateau, where the snowmelt that feeds the spring begins. The NAU team now has to account for those effects.

“It’s a new twist to our study,” Sankey noted.

A new grant from Grand Canyon National Park will expand the mapping across the park. The university scheduled that work to start in early 2026.

LaSala and Sankey plan to use airborne lidar and decades of satellite data to map sinkholes on both sides of the canyon. They will also track how snowmelt has accumulated over the last 40 years.

“Understanding where the water sinks is critical for the infrastructure, the animals, the plants and the rest of the ecosystems that rely on these springs,” LaSala said. “They’re like oases.”

The study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6383. A rare giant moa egg is returning to New Zealand after spending sixty years in an American collection

Colossal Biosciences announced plans to return a rare giant moa egg, discovered in New Zealand in 1966.

A giant moa egg found in New Zealand on January 14, 1966, spent about six decades in a private American collection. On June 12, 2026, it resurfaced at a public auction run by Artemis Gallery in Louisville, Colorado.

Colossal Biosciences, a Dallas-based biotechnology company whose de-extinction projects include the moa, bought the egg. On October 20, 2026, it announced plans to return it to Aotearoa, the Māori name for New Zealand.

Fewer than 40 sufficiently complete moa eggs are known in public collections worldwide. Only eight keep at least 90 percent of their shell.

The egg measures about 8.7 by 6.7 inches (22 by 17 centimeters). That is roughly 1.5 times the length of an ostrich egg and nearly double its volume.

It has been reconstructed from many fragments, and more pieces still need to be reattached.

The egg may have come from a human burial site from the Moa Hunter period, around AD 1300. Further research is needed to confirm that origin.

Colossal made the announcement at the opening of the 11th International Meeting of the Society of Avian Palaeontology and Evolution. The meeting ran from October 19 to 23 at the Christchurch Town Hall and opened with a pōwhiri, a Māori welcome.

Sir Peter Jackson, the filmmaker and a partner in Colossal’s moa program, contacted the company on learning the egg was being sold abroad. Colossal offered to rescue it at its own expense and fly it home privately.

“Every New Zealander grows up knowing the moa and feeling its loss,” Jackson said in a statement.

Once restored, the egg “will very likely become only the ninth known nearly intact moa egg,” Jackson noted.

Colossal plans a repatriation ceremony in December. The egg will be handed to Professor Te Maire Tau, a Māori historian and tribal leader in the Canterbury region.

“When we launched the moa program we made a clear commitment that indigenous leadership would guide the science and every decision surrounding the project,” explained Ben Lamm, the CEO and co-founder of Colossal.

“We are honored to help return it home,” Lamm stated.

The remaining fragments will be reattached under the guidance of Ngāi Tahu researchers.

Non-destructive imaging, or sampling for DNA and isotopes, could confirm the egg’s species and origin. Ngāi Tahu will decide whether and when to do this, following tikanga, or Māori customary practice.

Kyle Davis is a Ngāi Tahu archaeologist and an expert in cultural heritage.

“To see an egg of this rarity return to Te Waipounamu is extraordinary. It carries information about the moa species that birthed it, the landscape it came from and potentially the people connected to it,” Davis said.

Te Waipounamu is the Māori name for New Zealand’s South Island, where the egg is headed.

The moa de-extinction program behind the purchase began in 2025 as a joint initiative of Colossal, the Ngāi Tahu Research Centre, Jackson and Canterbury Museum.

Fossil eggshell preserves ancient DNA from extinct moa, elephant birds and emus, a study of fossil eggshell by Murdoch University researchers showed in 2010. Moa shell carried roughly 125 times less bacterial DNA than moa bone.

A team led by Leon Huynen recovered DNA from the inner and outer surfaces of moa eggs. Sequences from 69 eggshells matched seven moa species.

Several thin-shelled eggs belonged to the heaviest moa, in the genera Dinornis, Euryapteryx and Emeus. They were the most fragile bird eggs measured to date, the team reported in a 2010 study of moa eggs.

Sex-specific DNA on the outer surfaces of Dinornis and Euryapteryx eggs suggests that the lighter males incubated them. Even so, breakage would have been common if they sat on the eggs in the usual way.

The same DNA revealed two distinct lineages within Euryapteryx, whose eggs differed in shell thickness.

Each moa egg “holds information we can get nowhere else,” pointed out Beth Shapiro, Ph.D., Colossal’s chief science officer.

The Canterbury Museum lists nine described moa species, in six genera and three families. In the coastal moa, females could reach 4.9 feet (1.5 meters) tall, while males were about the size of a turkey.

People reached New Zealand more than 600 years ago, and moa disappeared within 100 to 300 years of their arrival.

Frequent hunting of the birds and their eggs drove those losses, a 2025 modeling study by Curtin University and University of Adelaide researchers suggests.

Moa could only have survived alongside people if no-take harvest zones had covered more than half of New Zealand’s land.

Dr. Paul Scofield, senior curator of natural history at Canterbury Museum, is a collaborating scientist on Colossal’s moa work.

“Moa are central to the natural and cultural history of Aotearoa, and this egg has far greater scientific and cultural value here than it could ever have in a private collection overseas,” Scofield remarked.

The information was obtained from Colossal Biosciences.

#6382. Researchers designed a stiff new solid that keeps heat from escaping better than soft foams and aerogels

A solid crystal film with organic layers blocks heat nearly as well as still air, while staying stiffer than most plastics, a record for dense solids.

The best heat blockers are mostly made of air. Inside foam, it sits trapped in tiny pockets, which is why foam insulates so well and also why it squashes so easily. Now, engineers and chemists have made a solid crystal film that is stiff and has no air pockets at all.

It blocks heat nearly as well as still air, while staying stiffer than most plastics.

According to the team, no fully dense solid had ever been measured blocking heat this well at room temperature. The result suggests stiffness and insulation don’t have to be traded against each other.

Jun Liu, an engineer at North Carolina State University, led the work with physicist Dali Sun. Chemists at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and colleagues in China also took part.

So far the stiff crystal film exists only in the lab. It is a layer far thinner than a human hair on silicon wafers, and it contains lead.

In most materials, stiffness and heat flow rise together. Strong bonds hold diamond together, and it is extremely rigid, and it carries heat very well. Plastics are made of loosely stuck chains, which makes them softer and poorer at passing heat along.

“Because, in general, stiff materials are good at conducting heat, and materials that are not stiff are good at insulating against heat,” Sun said.

That’s why most insulation is soft. Foams and aerogels get close to air by being mostly air. However, they give up almost all their stiffness to do it.

Better insulation is one way to save energy in buildings, but a coating that has to hold its shape on a circuit or a solar panel can’t be that fragile.

The stiff film belongs to a family of layered crystals called inorganic-organic perovskites that stack thin sheets of lead and iodine between layers of organic, carbon-based molecules.

In earlier work, Liu’s group found that swapping some of the carbon-carbon chains in the organic layers with benzene rings – stiff, six-sided rings of carbon atoms – made the crystals both stiffer and worse at carrying heat.

This time the team used molecules carrying two rings joined by a double bond. The rings make the layer rigid. They also vibrate mostly at high frequencies, which barely overlap with the vibrations of the lead-iodide sheets, so heat has trouble crossing from one layer to the next.

The longer molecules also jumble the way the sheets stack. That disorder slows the passage of heat even more.

The team compared four versions. The one with a plain carbon chain carried about five times the heat as the best version, which used a molecule called azobenzene ethyl ammonium.

To test the films, the researchers coated each one with a thin layer of metal. A short laser pulse heated the surface, and a second beam tracked how fast that heat drained away into the film below.

At room temperature, the best film carried heat only about 60 percent better than still air. That’s less than half as well as typical plastics, and one spot on one sample came in lower still.

The team got its best results from films about 6 millionths of an inch (150 nanometers) thick. Thinner and thicker films did worse, and only films in a narrow band of thicknesses stayed near the record.

Measurements at several spots on several samples gave consistent results, so the team doesn’t think it was a fluke of one sample.

For the second test, the team pressed a tiny vibrating probe against the film to measure how much it resisted bending. The azobenzene film came out stiffer than most plastics and far stiffer than foams and aerogels.

The films are made by spinning a liquid onto a surface and then heating it. The authors wrote that the method can be adapted to coat large or flexible surfaces cheaply. This is in contrast to earlier, ultralow-heat films that needed a high-vacuum chamber.

In an interview with Earth.com, Liu picked out two early targets for this technology. “Electronics and spacecraft would be the first series of applications, for the near-room-temperature thermal insulation in the form of thin film coating,” he said.

The team also sees it as a coating for use near room temperature, based on how it held up when heated.

The researchers see other possible roles too, such as shielding parts in fuel cells and solar collectors, or slowing the heat that spreads when a battery fails. None of those uses has been tested.

Like the materials in many experimental perovskite solar cells, the film is built around lead.

“Yes, the current formula has lead in it and there needs to be environmental considerations if the exact composition will be used,” Liu told Earth.com.

He called the tested film an example of a design idea, and he pointed to related crystals made without lead as the route to practical use. Handling lead safely is already a question for perovskite solar recycling.

The team also spelled out limits of the design idea. A near-twin molecule, with the two rings joined by carbon atoms instead of nitrogen, didn’t jumble the layers nearly as much and missed the record.

The team’s model accounts for that gap only loosely, and it can’t yet predict which molecule will work before someone makes it.

Nobody has shown whether a lead-free crystal keeps the same trick. By the team’s own estimate, a molecule whose rings twist more easily could push the film’s heat flow close to that of air itself. Making one is the next test.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6381. A whale buried for 9.5 million years had unexpected company

Scientists discovered ancient brittle star fossils beside whale bones, revealing how marine animals gathered around carcasses millions ago.

Brittle stars gather around dead whales on today’s seafloor, sometimes at much higher densities than on the surrounding seabed. Yet no fossil had ever placed them at a whale carcass.

Studies of fossil whale carcasses have mostly reported clams, snails, and animals that eat bone.

Now fossils from beside a beaked whale skeleton in Denmark suggest that brittle stars joined these gatherings 9.5 million years ago.

If that reading holds, it’s the first fossil record of a brittle star tied to a whale fall. That’s the term scientists use for a sunken whale carcass and the community of life it feeds.

The clues are tiny skeletal plates from a species new to science, now named Ophiura huebnerjenseni. The fossils are loose pieces rather than whole animals, so they can’t show what the brittle stars ate.

Ben Thuy, curator of paleontology at Luxembourg’s National Museum of Natural History, led the study.

Thuy worked with Mette Elstrup and Trine Sørensen of Museum Sønderjylland in Denmark. The fourth author, Lea Numberger-Thuy, works at the Luxembourg museum and at a dinosaur park in Germany.

The Gram Clay Pit in southern Denmark exposes about 23 to 25 feet (7 to 7.5 meters) of clay that built up on the floor of an ancient North Sea. Geologists call these layers the Gram Formation.

The pit is famous for its fossil clams, snails, and animals with backbones, including whale skeletons and giant megalodon vertebrae. Sea urchins, sea stars, and their relatives have been far scarcer there.

Scientists call that group of spiny-skinned animals the echinoderms. Before this study, only one echinoderm species had been reported from the Gram Formation.

Brittle stars are echinoderms too, with long, thin, flexible arms built from many small skeletal pieces.

The North Sea has plenty of them today, yet none had been found in these old clays. Thuy and Numberger-Thuy had already searched for them in clays of a similar age at Groß Pampau in northern Germany, without success.

The new fossils came from sediment collected in 2018, during the excavation of a beaked whale‘s lower jaw and four vertebrae from its backbone.

The bones were found about 21 feet (6.5 meters) below the top of the exposed clay. That level dates to roughly 9.5 million years ago.

Five sediment samples came from around the skeleton. The team dried each one, soaked it in water, and washed it through screens, then washed the leftovers a second time with a detergent-like chemical.

Under a microscope, the researchers picked out the smallest fossils one by one. The best brittle-star pieces were then photographed with a scanning electron microscope.

For comparison, they also processed a sample packed with tiny fossils. It came from 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) below a fossil log that was dug up in 2023.

“Only three samples taken directly beside the whale bones contained brittle-star remains. Samples from the same layer farther from the skeleton, and other comparison samples, yielded none,” Thuy said.

The three samples held 33 skeletal pieces in all. Most were plates from the sides of the arms, along with one piece of an arm’s inner backbone and one plate from the central disc of the body.

The arm plate chosen as the reference specimen for the species came from a sample taken 2 to 8 inches (5 to 20 centimeters) from the whale’s jawbones. Its shape placed the animal in the genus Ophiura, which still lives in the North Sea.

The closest living match there is Ophiura albida. The fossil plates differ from it in two ways: they have a slanted upper edge, and they lack the faint spurs that O. albida plates carry.

A cluster of fossils beside a skeleton doesn’t automatically mean the animals lived there, so the team considered other explanations.

“We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them,” Thuy added.

“However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass.”

Scientists divide a whale fall’s life into stages. In the early stage, the carcass enriches the seabed around it and feeds animals that take advantage of any sudden meal.

In the deep sea, later stages can follow. One of them supports life that runs on sulfur compounds released as the bones decay.

Fossils around the Gram whale included clams that filter food from the water and meat-eating snails, some of them scavengers.

The team found no clams of the kind that live off chemical energy with help from bacteria. The bones had no animals cemented to their surfaces and showed no signs of burrowing.

“We found no evidence for the later sulfide-based community stages that can develop at deep-sea whale falls,” Elstrup said.

“The discovery therefore adds a rare fossil perspective on how animals responded to a large food source on an ancient shallow-water seabed.”

Ophiura huebnerjenseni honors Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, who founded the heavy metal festival Wacken Open Air. It joins a long line of species named after musicians, but this one comes with a geological link.

“The clay that accumulated on the bottom of the ancient North Sea not only preserved the remains of a 9.5-million-year-old brittle star, it also turns Wacken Open Air into the muddy battlefield renowned by metalheads worldwide,” Numberger-Thuy said.

Brittle stars have been found before beside the carcasses of ichthyosaurs, ancient sea reptiles, in rocks from the Early Jurassic. A fossil whale fall had never produced one.

The researchers can’t yet say whether this species lived only at whale carcasses.

They favor the idea that it lived on the surrounding seabed and gathered at the carcass in numbers large enough to leave a fossil trace.

Living brittle stars at shallow whale falls also come from the nearby seafloor. Finding plates of this species in ordinary Gram mud, far from any bones, would support that idea.

For now, the only place Ophiura huebnerjenseni has been found is the mud right beside one whale.

The full study was published in the journal Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie – Abhandlungen.

#6380. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6379. Bees make a natural plastic that starts breaking down in soil within months

Solitary bees make natural plastic that breaks down in soil, offering clues for designing less persistent synthetic materials.

A plastic wrapper may be useful for a few minutes, then stay in the environment for centuries. But a small bee makes a plastic-like material that starts breaking down in soil within months.

The bee, Colletes inaequalis, uses it to cover the inside of its underground nest. The material helps protect the young bee growing inside.

Researchers studied these nests in Tennessee. In fresh nests, plastic made up 73% of the lining’s weight, but four months later, that share had fallen to 40%.

Now the team wants to learn how the bee makes a material that is tough but still breaks down. The answer could help scientists make better plastics for everyday use.

Jonathan Coote, an assistant professor at Virginia Tech, led the study.

Laura Russo, who studies bees at the University of Tennessee, first told him about the material while he was a doctoral student there.

Coote kept studying it during his later research at the University of Minnesota. After joining Virginia Tech in 2025, he made it his main research focus.

Scientists identified the chemical makeup of the bee’s plastic more than 45 years ago. But for years afterward, few people studied it further.

Most bees live alone rather than in hives. This species, common in the eastern United States, digs tunnels in the ground and builds small rooms for its young.

The female covers each room with a thin, clear layer, which gives these insects the name cellophane bees. She adds pollen and nectar, lays one egg, and closes the room.

The young bee spends more than 90% of its life inside. The lining likely protects it and its food from water and fungus.

The lining contains silk and a natural plastic made by the female.

A gland connected to her stinger releases tiny, ring-shaped molecules, which join into long chains as she spreads them over the walls.

The bee’s material resembles polyethylene, a plastic widely used in packaging.

Polyethylene contains long chains of carbon atoms held together by strong bonds that are hard to break, even in industrial compost.

Only about 9% of the world’s plastic was recycled in 2022. Nearly a third is poorly managed and ends up in the environment, where it can break into tiny pieces called microplastics.

Scientists have tried making similar plastics with weaker links in their chains. Water or enzymes, natural substances that help chemical reactions happen, can break these links.

These materials are called polyesters, and the bee’s plastic belongs to this group. “This is a polyester that mimics polyethylene,” Coote said.

Even with weaker links, most lab-made versions barely break down.

Their chains pack closely together and keep water out, making the weaker links hard to reach.

The best-studied version lost only 18% of its weight after 280 days in industrial compost. It did not break down at all under milder conditions.

The bee’s nests offered a clue that its material was different. More than 10,000 nests can share one site, and bees may return to the same ground for decades.

Yet the old plastic linings do not seem to pile up. Something appears to break them down.

The team first tried to dissolve the bee’s plastic to study its chains. After two days in a solvent heated to 302°F (150°C), the material still held its shape and size.

This suggested that the chains were linked together like a net.

About 60% of the plastic also formed tightly packed areas called crystals, arranged like those in polyethylene.

Usually, these tightly packed areas make plastic harder to break down. So the bee’s material seemed to have the same features that cause trouble in lab-made plastics.

The researchers collected fresh nests in March 2023 in Hamblen County, eastern Tennessee.

They returned in July and October 2023 and February 2024, digging seven to 12 inches (17 to 30 centimeters) down to find them.

After four months, the linings could still bend and hold their shape. By about seven months, when the young bees had become adults, cracks had appeared.

By 11 months, the linings crumbled when handled roughly. They had not vanished, but they were falling apart.

At first, the lining was about 73% plastic and 27% silk by weight. After four months, plastic made up only 40% of the remaining lining.

Silk usually breaks down fairly quickly, so the team was surprised to find the plastic breaking down even faster.

Later, the balance changed less, suggesting both materials were then breaking down at roughly the same pace.

Tightly packed regions accounted for about 60% of the plastic initially and nearly 100% of the remaining plastic after four months. By 11 months, their share had fallen to 39%.

This suggests the looser parts broke down first. The tightly packed parts appear to have broken down later.

The answer may lie in the plastic’s tiny building blocks. Most are rings with 18 carbon atoms, while some have 20 or 22.

Mixing these sizes may spread the weaker links unevenly along the chains. That could leave more links where water and enzymes can reach them.

The tightly packed areas are also small and less orderly, which could help. Microbes in the nest may also play a part.

Another idea involves an enzyme in the bee’s saliva. It might help build the plastic, then help break it down later.

The researchers rinsed the linings three times and collected the liquid. They added a chemical that this kind of enzyme can break apart.

Liquid from both a new lining and a four-month-old lining broke down the chemical. This suggests enzymes could keep working in the nest for months.

But the test used only one new nest and one older nest. More tests are needed to find out what those enzymes actually do.

The team still does not know which explanation matters most. Each nest provides only a few milligrams of lining, so some tests ran just once or twice, and all the older nests came from one site.

“The goal is to be able to answer that and then engineer it into something that we can make at scale. I don’t see a future where we have these massive bee farms making all of our plastic products,” Coote said.

If the spacing of the weaker links is the key, scientists could try copying it. They want a useful plastic that can break down in soil after its job is done.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."
