#6376. For Over a Decade, They’ve Been the Face of the World’s Most Entrancing Treasure Hunt. Have They Finally Solved Oak Island’s Mystery?

There's gold in the water on Oak Island—but a maze of old tunnels is hiding where it’s coming from.

“Hundreds of thousands of dollars and the wits of the cleverest American engineers and college professors have been vainly spent in trying to solve the mystery of the Money Pits of Oak island and its sheltered haven, Mahone bay, Nova Scotia.”

Those words appeared in the pages of Popular Mechanics 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures.” In the century that followed, the amount of money and wits expended on the mystery of Oak Island has only grown.

Since 2014, the public faces of the Oak Island mystery have been Rick and Marty Lagina, the stars of HISTORY’s long-running series The Curse of Oak Island. Across more than 250 episodes, audiences have followed along with the brothers’ success and setbacks, their obsession and their frustrations. When they began, via an investment in Oak Island Tours in 2006, they were pursuing a quixotic dream inspired by an old magazine article, joining a pantheon of prospectors that included Hollywood stars like Errol Flynn and John Wayne, and at least one U.S. President (Franklin D. Roosevelt, who kept tabs on the developments on Oak Island throughout his life).

Now, heading into their fourteenth season (debuting on November 10 on the History Channel), the siblings from Michigan are striking a more retrospective tone, reflecting on their role in this centuries-long quest for answers and the colleagues they’ve lost along the way (the season premiere pays homage to the late Dan Blankenship, a longtime partner of the Laginas who spent more than 50 years searching Oak Island before his 2019 passing). Now, there’s a question that’s become just as pressing for the two men as the Oak Island mystery itself: “After all these years, what was it all for?”

Ahead of the new season, Rick and Marty Lagina sat down with Pop Mech to reflect on fourteen seasons of television, how treasure-seeking has changed over the centuries, and what keeps them, and audiences, returning to Oak Island and its mysterious Money Pit year after year.

Although the marketing for Season 14 has leaned heavily on a new discovery through which the Laginas’ “lifelong quest has finally paid off,” the brothers kept the details of the coming episodes close to the vest. (Pop Mech was able to preview only the season premiere.) Otherwise, they were as candid and at times as self-effacing as they’ve been throughout fourteen seasons of television.

In fact, Rick is quick to dispel what he feels is the biggest misconception fans of the show often have. “We’re portrayed on some level as experts in every field, and we’re not,” he told us. “That’s why we have such a large tent of people helping us, because we’re not experts in every field, every arena.”

“It’s a very complex mystery,” he adds, “and we need everybody under the tent, if you will.”

That tent doesn’t just include the various experts who appeared on the program over the last decade, but also the centuries of treasure hunters who came before them. “Rick holds those prior searchers in this huge, high regard,” Marty says of his brother, “and thinks about them all the time.”

If one believes the account published in The Yarmouth Herald in 1863, that list of prior searchers stretches all the way back to 1795. That’s when a young farmer named Daniel McGinnis arrived on Oak Island via canoe, propelled by a piece of folklore which claimed that Captain Kidd had buried millions of dollars worth of treasure on the island. As he searched, he came across a depression in the ground that seemed deliberate, and called together a small team to dig on the site. As they excavated to a depth of 30 feet, they found remnants of a previous presence at the site (some accounts say flagstones, others oak platforms), and that led them to think they’d discovered the location of the buried treasure—or what’s long been referred to as the “Money Pit.”

In the early 1800s, the Onslow Company reportedly paid a visit to the same site, and they dug deeper into the Money Pit than McGinnis ever dared to go, roughly 80 to 90 feet deep. The Onslow Company found further indications that the pit was deliberately dug to store something, though their evidence was far more destructive. Their dig set off a booby trap that caused the Money Pit to flood with seawater up to the 33-foot level. The Onslow Company was unable to bail out the excavation site at the time. To make matters worse, Marty would note, later attempts only exacerbated the problem.

“There was almost certainly a flood tunnel that caused the initial booby trap,” he told us, “And people will come up to you and they’ll say, well, why don’t you shut off the water this way or shut off the water that way. The problem is there’s been so much pumping over the years by other people that the water is coming in from other places.”

Marty, who possesses an extensive engineering background in both petroleum and renewable energy, is both enamored with and exasperated by what’s been left behind by the treasure hunters who preceded him.

“From an engineering standpoint, I’m always astonished, absolutely astonished and in rapt admiration for what those people were able to do with picks and shovels,” Marty says of those earlier excavators. “I mean, you can’t believe it. If you were out there, and you saw these hand hewn timbers come up from 180 feet down. They had nothing. They had horses, you know? I mean, it’s just really amazing.”

Impressive as that work was for its time, it left modern-day diggers with consequences of their own.

“One of our scientific consultants, Ian Spooner, is a PhD geologist. He calls it Chutes & Ladders,” Marty says, before quickly adding, “He actually calls it Snakes and Ladders, because that’s the Canadian thing.”

“We have so many interconnected passages now that have been made by other people that we have to decipher all that,” he laments, “And every time a timber comes out, I mean, almost every time, you have to say, is this an original worker’s timber or is this a searcher’s timber? And we have to run the scientific analysis on that.”

In the show’s ninth season, water samples from the site turned up trace amounts of gold, a discovery that showed just how badly booby traps and centuries of earlier digging had muddied the trail.

“If you followed [the show], you know there’s gold in the water, which has kept us coming back for years,” Marty continued, “Now it’s there, it’s real, it’s coming from a source. And if the water was just moving geologically, like I’m used to in my prior business, we could trace it back, but the problem is it’s all interconnected, so it’s difficult.”

Have past attempts to solve the mystery actually further obscured Oak Island’s secrets? Did stories stoking the hunger for treasure actually, if unintentionally, contribute to the partial destruction of the Nova Scotia island?

If so, it’s a guilt that Pop Mech partially shares.

At one point in our conversation, Marty cuts in to jokingly ask, “By the way, can I do a quick commercial for Popular Mechanics?” to which this author, never afraid of a little self-promotion, gleefully assented. “Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” he says, “And Rick will attest, we kind of had a hard time getting our hands on actual magazines. But I mean, I would read those from cover to cover.”

“There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” Rick chimed in to add, “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.”

As it turns out, there was more than one. But if Rick recalled an Oak Island story from one of the magazines he and Marty read cover to cover, it was likely the one published at the exact mid-point between 1926’s “Hunting Hidden Treasures” and today.

Fifty years ago, the September 1976 issue of Popular Mechanics ran with the cover story “7 Great Quests of Man,” and the mystery of Oak Island’s treasure was discussed alongside such cryptic quandaries (and just plain cryptids) as Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, ancient aliens, and Noah’s Ark.

But if such outlandish company makes the Oak Island mystery feel like a fantasy, the work the Laginas have done over fourteen seasons has pulled things back into the realm of reality. While a literal pot of gold at the end of this proverbial rainbow would be a satisfying conclusion, Rick says that the true value of these excavations extends beyond the potential payday.

“When you talk about story, the science and technology has pushed the timeline of what happened on Oak island, or at least when something started to happen on Oak Island, to me, has been pushed back, literally, into the latter part of the 13th century,” he noted, “We have core samples from wells, we have carbon dates from old walls, we have archaeo-astronomical alignments. I don’t see any other explanation that some of these structures, including Nolan’s Cross, given the alignments contained within them, were of that time frame. So what happened long, long ago, well before Europeans were supposed to be on this continent, to me, that’s a story in and of itself.”

Perhaps, in that sense, the treasure has served as the profit motive, the lure that funded centuries of expeditions, which may finally be uncovering the site’s true history.

“Marty has always said that the mystery of Oak Island has endured because of treasure, because of that component, and he’s absolutely right,” Rick concluded. “But at this point, I think the treasure and the story are somewhat aligned in terms of importance, and I hope that we can push forward on both agendas.”

The new season of The Curse of Oak Island premieres on the History Channel November 10 at 9/8c.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. #6375. When rain returns after a drought, groundwater reserves don’t always get caught up before the next drought

Most groundwater refills faster than it drains in a drought, but in about a quarter of places, the next drought hits before recovery ends.

When a drought breaks, the rain returns first, then the soil moisture, the plants and the rivers. Groundwater usually comes last, and in some places the next drought arrives before it has caught up.

A new global analysis suggests that, in most places, groundwater refills faster than it drains during a drought. But across about a quarter of the places studied, water levels tended to slip back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That matters because groundwater supplies roughly 35 percent of all the fresh water people withdraw, and it’s the reserve many communities rely on when rivers run low.

Hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth led the work with three colleagues at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. Their results come from a computer model rather than direct measurements.

It estimates how deep you’d have to dig to reach water, a level called the water table, month by month from 1960 to 2019.

This model divides the world’s land into squares about 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) across. It was developed at Utrecht’s Department of Physical Geography, and it tracks both the rain that soaks into soil and the water people pump out of it.

Checked against real wells, the model gave useful estimates at about 80 percent of wells shallower than about 200 feet (60 meters). For deeper wells, the figure was about 70 percent.

For every square and every calendar month, the team worked out how deep the water table usually was and how much that depth normally varied.

A drought started when the groundwater dropped so far below its usual level for that time of year that only about 16 percent of months would qualify. It ended when the water rose back above that line.

Droughts lasting two months or less were left out, because monthly data can’t capture them reliably. For the rest, the team measured how fast the water fell, how fast it rose again, and what it did in the six months afterward.

Climate did more than anything else to set the pace of recovery. Places where a lot of rain soaks into the ground, such as the Amazon and Southeast Asia, recovered quickly. Their droughts also tended to be shorter and more frequent.

Dry regions recovered slowly. The slow places included Australia, the Middle East and Central Asia, southern Africa, southern South America and the U.S. Midwest.

During drought recovery, the groundwater at a typical location rose about 0.7 inches (1.8 centimeters) a month. In the fastest places it climbed as much as about 3 feet (1 meter) a month.

Those raw speeds partly reflect how much a water table swings in an ordinary year. So the team also compared each place with its own normal range, and the split between wet and dry regions became sharper.

Average speed told only part of the story. Two places could recover at the same average rate and still behave very differently during a drought.

Hauswirth hadn’t expected recovery to vary so much within a single region. In an interview with Earth.com, she said, “I was surprised to see that the groundwater recovery pattern was not necessarily homogeneous within a region and could vary quite a bit locally.”

To capture those differences, the team sorted every location by how its droughts unfolded. About 57 percent were resilient: on average, the water came back faster than it had dropped. Another 26 percent were unstable, slipping back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That makes the unstable group the second largest. The researchers described its behavior as even more critical than that of the vulnerable group, where the water fell quickly and climbed back slowly.

The unstable group covered about 15 percent of places, and only around 2 percent were stable, with the fall and the rise at about the same speed.

Unstable places weren’t clustered in one part of the world, and they weren’t limited to heavily pumped areas. Their droughts were shorter, milder and more frequent than in any other group, often with little time to refill in between.

Terrain set the vulnerable places apart. In every region the team examined up close, they turned up at higher elevations, where the ground stores less water and the water table swings more widely.

In Europe, some may be linked to limestone country, where water drains through cracks and caves.

The close-ups included California, Spain, India and the North China Plain, all places known for heavy groundwater use. In Spain, the vulnerable and unstable spots shared similar pumping patterns. In California, pumping appeared to affect more of the categories.

Sorting places this way, Hauswirth said, made it clear that local features “are an important part of the drivers and should not be underestimated.”

For water managers in vulnerable regions, her advice starts with knowing where the water comes from. Where possible, she said, they should map how much of local demand and supply is covered by groundwater.

That “could help us better understand when groundwater resources are overexploited,” she told Earth.com, and when a wet spell could help restore levels, possibly by cutting back on pumping.

The authors name their own blind spots. They filtered out places where water tables have fallen steadily for decades, often from heavy pumping, because a long decline makes single droughts hard to pick out. Those places may be underrepresented in the results.

Every number here is also a model’s estimate. This model performed well against real wells, but global groundwater models have both overestimated and underestimated water levels in the past.

And because the team averaged 60 years together, the results can’t show whether recovery is speeding up or slowing down.

“I want to dive deeper into how these recovery patterns have changed over time, as the current work has mainly focused on the spatial pattern,” Hauswirth said.

Next, the team wants to pair the four categories with projections of a warmer climate. That could show which places are at risk of shifting from resilient toward vulnerable or unstable.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Water.

#6374. Semaglutide study raises new questions about pregnancy safety

A small sheep study found that semaglutide reduced maternal cardiac output, uterine blood flow, and fetal oxygen levels within two hours.

Semaglutide – the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy – can help people lose weight and reduce cardiovascular risk in certain patients.

Some women taking semaglutide will become pregnant before they know it.

Although human studies have examined pregnancy exposure, the potential effects on fetal development remain uncertain.

A new animal study from Adelaide University examines how a single dose affects maternal circulation and fetal oxygen levels in sheep.

Researchers gave a single dose of semaglutide to pregnant sheep and tracked what happened using phase-contrast MRI.

Within two hours, maternal cardiac output dropped significantly. Blood flow to the uterus fell with it. And oxygen levels in the fetal blood declined.

The study is small and preliminary – seven pregnant ewes, one acute dose. But the measurements are precise.

Researchers surgically catheterized the fetal femoral artery and the maternal jugular vein at 113–116 days of gestation.

They then performed MRI scans at 117–119 days to measure cardiac output and uterine artery blood flow at baseline, 20 minutes post-infusion, and two hours post-infusion. The dose was 0.75 mg of semaglutide.

Blood pressure didn’t change in the mothers or fetuses. Heart rates stayed steady.

But maternal cardiac output fell by 0.80 liters per minute at the two-hour mark compared to baseline.

Uterine blood flow remained the same proportion of maternal cardiac output, suggesting that its decline reflected the reduction in overall blood pumped by the mother’s heart.

Fetal oxygen levels told the rest of the story.

Partial pressure of oxygen in fetal arterial blood dropped from 23.25 mmHg at baseline to 19.94 at 45 minutes and 18.82 at two hours.

The decline from baseline was statistically significant at two hours.

“Within two hours of administering semaglutide, we found that the amount of blood pumped by the mother’s heart had significantly decreased, reducing blood flow to the uterus and lowering oxygen levels in the developing fetus,” said study co-author Mitchell Lock.

“Oxygen is essential for healthy fetal growth and development, so any reduction in its supply raises questions about what might happen if exposure to the drug continues throughout pregnancy.”

Those are acute effects from a single dose. This experiment did not assess the effects of repeated exposure.

Semaglutide is not recommended during pregnancy. Product labeling advises stopping semaglutide at least two months before a planned pregnancy.

That guidance assumes people plan their pregnancies – which, of course, many don’t.

A 2025 KFF poll found that 12% of US adults were currently taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss or other health conditions.

In Australia, around half a million people take them for diabetes alone, and the real number including off-label weight loss use is likely much higher.

Here’s the bind. Some women will be reluctant to stop because they don’t want to regain weight.

Others taking the drug for diabetes may worry about destabilizing their blood sugar management. And some will simply conceive before they realize they should have stopped.

“While weight-loss medications have become incredibly popular, there’s still a lot we don’t know about how they might affect a developing baby,” Lock said.

This is a sheep study that gave a single acute dose to seven animals. The results show what happens in the first two hours, not across an entire pregnancy.

The mechanism – reduced cardiac output leading to reduced uterine flow and fetal oxygenation – is plausible and physiologically coherent, but it hasn’t been demonstrated in humans.

“Our findings suggest a potential risk to fetal development, but we haven’t yet established whether these short-term changes affect fetal growth, what happens over a longer period of semaglutide use or whether similar effects could occur in human pregnancies,” said coauthor Janna Morrison.

“With the growing popularity of GLP-1 medications, it’s important that we better understand their potential effects during pregnancy so women and healthcare professionals can make informed and safe decisions about their use.”

The study doesn’t prove semaglutide harms human fetuses. It found that a single dose was followed by lower fetal arterial oxygen pressure in pregnant sheep.

The findings raise questions about whether repeated exposure could affect fetal growth and whether similar circulatory changes occur in humans.

Human pregnancy studies have not established a consistent increase in major birth defects following semaglutide exposure, but the available evidence remains limited.

This small sheep study adds a physiological finding that warrants further investigation.

The findings were reported in a conference abstract in the journal Heart, Lung and Circulation.

#6372. Tiny sparrows hold ancient clues to human heart disease

A detailed map of sparrow heart cells reveals similarities with human hearts and clues to how birds adapt to life at high altitude.

A tiny sparrow has more in common with us than you’d think – at least when it comes to the heart.

Scientists have built the first single-cell atlas of a wild bird’s heart, analyzing more than 200,000 cells and nuclei from newborn and adult Eurasian tree sparrows.

What they found is a remarkably conserved cardiac blueprint.

Similar core cell types, gene activity patterns, and disease-linked pathways – shared across species separated by 300 million years of evolution.

The study was led by researchers at the Institute of Zoology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Scientists compared heart cells from sparrows living at sea level in Cangzhou (10 meters altitude) and high on the Tibetan Plateau at Gahai (3,400 meters).

The team, led by Yan Hao, Xiang Zhou, and Qingshuo Zhao, sequenced 168,634 neonatal cells and 33,694 adult nuclei.

Eleven major cardiac cell types showed up in sparrow hearts. These include cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and immune cells.

That’s similar to what we find in mice and humans. But the proportions shift dramatically between life stages.

Cardiomyocytes, the heart’s muscle cells, accounted for 22% of the neonatal sample and 11% of the adult sample.

Endothelial cells, which line blood vessels, accounted for 13% of the neonatal sample and 31% of the adult sample.

The baby heart is built for rapid growth. The adult heart is built for endurance – a dense network to keep blood and oxygen flowing under sustained demand.

Using a computational tool called CAME, the researchers mapped sparrow heart cells against those of mice and humans. Matching rates ranged from 86.7% to 99.5%.

Cardiomyocytes were the most conserved cell type of all, with cross-species gene expression correlations between 0.57 and 0.62. That’s a tight overlap for animals that last shared an ancestor before dinosaurs went extinct.

Fibroblasts and endothelial cells were more species-specific, with human-sparrow correlations dropping to 0.23–0.24.

That makes biological sense. Heart muscle cells must meet strict demands for electrical signaling and contraction.

Supporting cells like fibroblasts have more freedom to adapt to each species’ particular mechanical environment.

The team didn’t stop at cataloging cell types. They asked whether the genes conserved across species also happen to be the ones that go wrong in human heart disease.

The answer was a strong yes. In adult hearts, genes linked to known human cardiac pathologies showed tight expression correlations between tree sparrows and both mice and humans.

The sparrow-human correlations (0.53 to 0.66) were statistically comparable to mouse-human correlations (0.52 to 0.72).

That’s a remarkable finding. The similarities suggest that sparrows could help researchers investigate biological pathways involved in human heart disease.

Sparrows living at 3,400 meters face a persistent shortage of oxygen, known as chronic hypoxia.

Their hearts are larger, with more blood vessels, a typical high-altitude adaptation.

At the cellular level, those adaptations diverge sharply by age. Adult high-altitude cardiomyocytes showed 191 differentially expressed genes, mostly tied to cardiac muscle development.

Neonatal ones showed only 22, focused instead on energy metabolism. Just two genes overlapped.

While baby hearts at altitude appear to prioritize energy metabolism under limited oxygen, adult hearts emphasize structural changes. So they respond to the same stressor differently depending on life stage.

Among the altitude-adaptation genes, one stood out: IGF1R. It encodes a receptor in the insulin-like growth factor pathway and sits at a hub connecting MAPK signaling, cytoskeletal organization, and cardiac muscle contraction.

It’s already known to drive heart enlargement in mice and humans. The researchers found it upregulated in high-elevation sparrow cardiomyocytes too.

To test whether it actually causes hypertrophy in birds, they overexpressed IGF1R in chicken cardiomyocyte cultures.

The cells grew significantly larger, with elevated levels of hypertrophy markers NPPA and ACTA1.

Gene activity changes were consistent with involvement of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway.

Growth-promoting genes like BDNF, BCL2, and MYC went up.

The study used different sequencing technologies for neonates and adults, which could introduce technical artifacts when comparing life stages.

The IGF1R experiments were done in cell culture, not living birds. So the gene is a plausible contributor to high-altitude heart growth, but not yet a confirmed driver in vivo.

And while the sparrow-human gene correlations are impressive, they were somewhat weaker in neonatal hearts. This suggests developmental trajectories diverge more than adult endpoints do.

The bigger picture is about what hearts share after 300 million years of going their separate evolutionary ways.

Birds and mammals independently evolved four-chambered hearts as well as endothermy. And now it turns out they built them with strikingly similar molecular machinery.

That shared regulatory logic means sparrows could become a useful model for human cardiovascular disease.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation Life.

#6371. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6370. Cat urine may hold an early warning of kidney disease

A protein in cat urine may help detect kidney disease earlier, while other protein patterns could reveal different types of damage.

Kidney disease is common in cats, but vets often find it late. The usual blood test may still look normal after a cat has lost more than a third of its kidney function.

Now, researchers have found a possible early warning sign in cat urine. A protein called MMP-7 was higher in cats at the earliest stage of the disease.

The study also found three groups of sick cats with different patterns of urine proteins. This suggests that cats with the same diagnosis may have different kinds of kidney damage.

Katelyn Brusach led the work in Jessica Quimby’s feline kidney research program at The Ohio State University College of Veterinary Medicine.

Her team compared urine from 30 healthy cats and 34 cats with chronic kidney disease, including just five at the earliest stage.

Estimates of how common chronic kidney disease, or CKD, is in cats vary widely. It is especially common in older cats.

CKD means the kidneys have lost some of their ability to work, and that loss lasts over time.

The damage can begin in the kidneys’ filters, their tiny tubes, or the tissue around them.

Vets usually measure creatinine in the blood to diagnose CKD and judge its stage. This substance comes from muscles, so when a sick cat loses muscle, the reading can look falsely low.

Creatinine and another blood marker called SDMA can reliably identify middle and late stages, the researchers wrote, but early disease is harder to spot.

Knowing exactly what kind of damage has occurred requires a kidney biopsy, which is not always possible.

Vets use substances in blood or urine as clues to disease. Researchers call these substances biomarkers.

“The search for more precise biomarkers is not unique to feline CKD,” Brusach said. “This is a common problem in biomarker discovery across other chronic diseases.”

Her team turned to urine because it comes directly from the kidneys. Changes in its proteins could offer clues about changes inside those organs.

All 64 cats in the study were pets enrolled during clinical exams at Ohio State. The cats with CKD had stable disease.

The researchers classified the sick cats using the International Renal Interest Society‘s four-stage system.

Five had stage one disease, 15 had stage two, eight had stage three, and six had stage four, the most severe.

They examined each urine sample with a mass spectrometer, a machine that identifies molecules by their mass. This let them look at many proteins at once.

The team identified 2,219 different proteins. As far as the researchers knew, no earlier study had used this method to identify so many proteins in cat urine.

The team first compared the five cats at stage one with the 30 healthy cats. Several proteins differed between the two groups.

Only MMP-7 also tracked creatinine levels across all 64 cats. Cats with higher creatinine, a sign that their kidneys were working less well, tended to have more MMP-7 in their urine.

MMP-7 is an enzyme that breaks down material around cells.

Researchers think its family of enzymes plays a role in kidney scarring, but they disagree about whether these enzymes add to scarring or help limit it.

An earlier study of cat kidneys found that genes for three enzymes in this family were more active in diseased tissue, but only MMP-7 was linked to creatinine.

Brusach’s team suggested that MMP-7 may offer an early sign of kidney scarring.

Kidney disease can look different from one cat to the next, making it hard for one protein to tell the whole story.

“Chronic diseases are often heterogeneous, which makes them challenging to encapsulate with one protein,” Brusach said.

The team compared the full mix of urine proteins from each cat. Healthy cats grouped together, but some cats with early CKD fell into that same group.

The researchers suggested that early disease may not yet change many urine proteins, or that standard tests missed disease in some apparently healthy cats.

Some cats initially classified as healthy later received a CKD diagnosis.

The remaining cats with CKD fell into three groups separate from the healthy cats. These groups offered possible clues to different kinds of damage.

One group included five cats: four with stage two disease and one with stage three. The researchers found no distinctive pattern of urine proteins in this group.

The researchers suggested that these cats might have a more stable form of the disease, might not yet have worsened, or might have normally aging kidneys.

Scientists still do not fully understand why some cats get worse while others do not. In a 2012 study cited by the team, 81% of cats at stage two did not reach stage four before they died.

A second group contained five younger male cats with advanced disease.

Their urine had higher levels of proteins involved in immune responses and blood clotting, and all five had excess protein in their urine.

The team suspected that the immune system was causing inflammation in the kidneys’ filters, an uncommon problem in cats.

Without biopsies, though, they could not confirm that explanation.

The third group included seven cats with high levels of a different set of proteins. Some of those proteins occur in the membranes around cells.

This pattern may point to damage in the cells lining the kidneys’ tiny tubes. The researchers suggested it could reflect the usual form of late-stage CKD.

The study included few cats at stage one or stage four and few elderly cats with healthy kidneys. Healthy cats averaged 6.4 years old, while cats with CKD averaged 11.3.

Age or sex may have influenced the groups, but the study was not designed to test either factor.

The researchers also cannot yet say how well MMP-7 or any of the protein patterns would work as a test.

The team called for future studies that directly measure the proteins it identified.

For MMP-7, a larger and more varied group of cats would help show whether it can reliably tell early disease apart from healthy kidneys.

Zoetis Inc. funded the work through a sponsored research agreement with Quimby’s lab.

The study is published in the Journal of Proteome Research.

A double subduction zone off the coast of Japan caused rifting halfway around the world to accelerate, fueling the formation of some of North America's most iconic features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A geological reorganization near Japan may have led to the formation of one of North America's most recognizable features.

The birth of the Gulf of California, which rifted from Mexico and created the Baja Peninsula 6 million to 8 million years ago, was accelerated by the formation of a double subduction zone more than 6,000 miles (9,600 kilometers) away, near Japan. This reorganization led to a transfer of tectonic force across the Pacific tectonic plate, which, in turn, opened the Gulf of California and ultimately led to the Grand Canyon's formation, according to new research published Oct. 29 in the journal Science.

The findings will help researchers understand more about plate boundaries, which is where most of the strongest earthquakes on the planet originate.

"It's more than a regional curiosity," study co-author Thorsten Becker, a geophysicist at the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin), told Live Science. "It's a reminder of the global connectedness of mantle convection and plate tectonics."

The Gulf of California is an example of a rift zone, a place where continental crust pulls apart and creates a spot so low that it can be filled by ocean water. There are many rift zones around the world; a currently active one is the Red Sea. But rifting can slow down, speed up or peter out entirely. In the Gulf of California, rifting not only persisted, but sped up. Rifting took about 6 million to 13 million years ‪—‬ much quicker than the typical speed of 30 million to 80 million years.

Study co-author Guido Gianni, a geophysicist at the Czech Academy of Sciences, wondered why that was. No previous research fully explained the rapid rifting, which changed the face of North America in many ways. Not only did the rifting transfer Baja California to the Pacific Plate, but it provided an outlet for the developing Colorado River, which subsequently carved the Grand Canyon on its way to sea level.

Gianni and Becker's doctoral student at UT Austin, Xiang He, used a global model of plate tectonics, run on supercomputers at the Texas Advanced Computing Center on campus, to find out if far-flung forces might provide an explanation. Around the same time the Gulf of California was pulling apart, Japan was undergoing its own geological changes. Off the coast of Japan, the Pacific Plate subducts, or pushes under, the Eurasian Plate. About 10 million to 12 million years ago, a single subduction zone near Japan transitioned into two separate subduction zones.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A double subduction zone off Japan (left inset) accelerated the growth of the Gulf of California (right inset).

This transition at the western end of the Pacific Plate influenced the tectonic forces on the other side of the plate, He, Gianni, Becker and their colleagues found.

"It turned out — ta-da! — [with] the change in this pulling stress, Baja California was one of the few places outside the Japan region that were affected," Becker said. It was "unexpected and sort of a little bit too good to be true."

The researchers tweaked their model to see if the result held with different assumptions about stresses and mantle properties, and it did.

The Gulf of California was already rifting regardless of the situation across the Pacific. The initial rift was caused by the subduction of a tectonic plate called the Farallon Plate, located under the West Coast of North America. The Farallon slab stretched and thinned the continental crust of the North American plate as it moved. But such rifting might have ended with nothing more than the formation of a little valley or low spot if Japan's influence had not kicked in to give the rifting some extra oomph.

The findings have a direct effect on scientists' understanding of how plate boundaries form, Becker said. And this isn't just academic. The findings could have implications for understanding earthquake-generating faults such as the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest, Becker said. Cascadia is what's known as a "megathrust" boundary, capable of triggering quakes of more than magnitude 9.

"If I'm asking what is the mantle doing underneath Cascadia so I get our megathrust correct," Becker said, "I need to include these effects."

Gianni, G. M., He, X., Becker, T. W., & Faccenna, C. (2026). Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting. Science, 394(6823), 515–519. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef5187

#6367. Saharan dust brings unexpected passengers to the Amazon rainforest

Saharan dust carried a distinct bacterial community across the Atlantic to the Amazon rainforest, where airborne endotoxin levels roughly tripled.

The air above the Amazon rainforest looks calm from the ground. Under a microscope, it’s teeming with pollen, fungal spores, plant debris, and bacteria.

The fungal community is usually remarkably stable, while bacterial communities vary with height and time. But during five days in February 2020, something foreign arrived.

Saharan dust, blown across the Atlantic over ten days, carried with it an entirely different bacterial community. Its arrival also coincided with a threefold increase in airborne endotoxins.

The study was led by Jens Weber and Bettina Weber at the University of Graz in Austria.

They worked with researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry and a network of Brazilian partner institutions.

The scientists collected aerosol samples at the Amazon Tall Tower Observatory.

This is a 325-meter research tower surrounded by hundreds of kilometers of unbroken primary rainforest in Brazil’s Uatumã Sustainable Development Reserve.

Africa’s drylands are the planet’s single biggest dust source. They pump 11 to 15 teragrams of mineral particles into the atmosphere each year – roughly half the global total.

Those plumes regularly cross the Atlantic, depositing phosphorus and iron that fertilize the Amazon basin.

What wasn’t clear was which microbes the dust carried and how its arrival affected the air over the rainforest.

The team installed high-volume dust filter samplers at two heights on the ATTO tower: 42 meters, within the forest canopy, and 323 meters, well above it.

They collected filters daily from 10 February to 2 March 2020, then ran genetic analyses to characterize the bacterial and fungal communities in the samples.

The five-day dust event hit between 18 and 22 February. Backward trajectory modeling confirmed the air masses had traveled from North Africa.

The change was dramatic. Mean aerosol mass concentrations jumped nearly eightfold – from about 2.7 micrograms per cubic meter under normal conditions to over 21 micrograms during the dust event, peaking at 45.78.

The particles’ calcium content was consistent with Saharan mineral dust.

Under normal conditions, the bacterial community at 42 meters reflected local canopy sources – microbes associated with bark, leaves, and lichens.

At 323 meters, it picked up more long-range material. But during the dust intrusion, bacterial communities at both heights converged sharply toward the same profile: organisms associated with dryland soils, biological soil crusts, and marine environments.

Endospore-forming bacteria belonging to the phylum Bacillota – minor players under background conditions – became the dominant feature at both heights.

The researchers identified a distinct signature of terrestrial soil genera including Clostridium, Brevibacillus, and Tumebacillus.

Cyanobacteria characteristic of biocrusts – Schizothrix and Trichocoleus – showed up too.

Marine bacteria made the journey as well. Synechococcus, detected roughly 1,000 kilometers from the nearest coastline, illustrated the dust plume’s capacity to scoop up ocean microbes during its transatlantic passage.

The fungi, by contrast, barely noticed. Wood-decomposing Basidiomycota dominated at both heights before, during, and after the dust event.

At 42 meters, they made up 93.8% of fungal sequences.

The researchers suggest that abundant local spores may have masked any fungal material arriving from Africa.

“Soils in arid regions and deserts are largely colonized by microbial communities, known as biological soil crusts,” Bettina Weber said.

“Genetically, the bacteria match organisms from the Sahara, which proves that they are transported from African biocrusts across the Atlantic by wind all the way to Brazil’s rainforest.”

The most immediately concerning finding wasn’t a particular species. It was endotoxins – lipopolysaccharides found in the outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria, released when those bacteria die.

They’re chemically stable, resistant to heat, and capable of triggering inflammation in humans.

Endotoxin concentrations at 323 meters roughly tripled during the dust event, rising from 0.45 to 1.27 endotoxin units per cubic meter, with a peak of 2.10.

The levels correlated tightly with coarse-mode aerosol mass.

The researchers traced the signal to two Gram-negative sources: dead microbial material from African dryland soils and marine cell-wall debris picked up over the ocean.

“I was surprised by the large amount of endotoxins in the air,” Jens Weber said.

“Previous studies in the Caribbean have shown that asthma attacks often increase when Saharan dust arrives. Whether a similar correlation exists in the Amazon remains to be investigated.”

Those endotoxins are relevant not just for the forest ecosystem but for roughly 3.9 million people in Brazil’s Amazonas state, plus riverside and coastal communities sitting in the plume’s path.

One critical gap is that the study can’t tell us whether the bacteria are still alive. Amplicon sequencing detects genetic material regardless of whether the organism is viable or dead.

Endotoxins trigger immune responses either way – dead bacteria are perfectly capable of causing inflammation.

But whether intact, living microorganisms survive ten days of UV radiation, desiccation, and temperature swings over the open Atlantic is a separate question.

The team plans follow-up work using fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry to test viability directly.

There’s also the matter of pathogens. Obligate pathogens weren’t enriched during the dust event.

Some opportunistic genera – Staphylococcus and Clostridium – did increase at 323 meters.

However, identification at the genus level could not establish whether disease-causing species were present.

The dust appears to deliver soil bacteria and immunostimulatory debris rather than an army of infectious agents.

That distinction matters, though it won’t be fully settled until viability testing catches up.

The study is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

#6366. Scientists tracked millions of phones to uncover patterns in carbon emissions

Scientists used anonymized cell phone mobility data to estimate carbon emissions, testing the approach across four countries.

When COVID-19 lockdowns froze the planet in early 2020, carbon emissions plummeted almost overnight.

The problem? The instruments tracking those emissions couldn’t keep up.

Conventional inventories lag reality by months. Satellite inversions come with their own trade-offs between resolution and coverage.

A new study explores another approach: using people’s movements to help estimate carbon emissions.

The research was led by Mengning Wang and Xin Lu from China’s National University of Defense Technology.

Collaborators included Xiaoling Zhang from the University of Hong Kong and scholars from various international institutions.

The researchers turned anonymized cell phone signals from 318 million Chinese mobile users into what amounts to a near-real-time carbon meter.

They tested the framework across four countries.

Commuting, deliveries, business trips, and holiday travel often generate carbon emissions.

The researchers reasoned that if so many carbon-producing processes involve physically moving people and goods, then the movement itself might serve as a fast measuring stick.

They took anonymized signaling data from China Unicom and converted it into daily intercity mobility networks.

Each city became a node and each flow of people between cities became an edge.

From these networks they extracted structural features – how central a city is, how tightly clustered its connections are, how many links it maintains – and combined those with population and geographic data.

Then they trained machine learning models against the GRACED dataset, which tracks daily CO2 emissions across seven sectors: power, industry, residential consumption, ground transport, domestic aviation, international aviation, and shipping.

The window researchers studied was January and February 2020. It’s hard to imagine a harder test.

Spring Festival travel sent 68.74 million daily intercity trips surging through the network. Then lockdowns hit.

Mobility crashed by 71.3%. Multi-source carbon emissions dropped from an average of roughly 356.5 million kilograms of carbon per day to a minimum of 209.6 million – a 41.2% collapse. The whole thing happened in weeks.

And yet the correlation between daily national mobility and CO2 emissions held firm at r = 0.89. At the city level, it was a more modest but still significant r = 0.49.

The best-performing model – LightGBM, a tree-based ensemble – achieved R² values of 1.00 for multi-source emissions, 0.99 for domestic aviation, and 0.98 for ground transportation across 366 cities and 60 days.

Those are extraordinary numbers for something as messy as urban carbon output.

The real surprise came when the framework crossed borders.

Using open-source mobility datasets, the team applied the same approach to Italy, the continental United States, and Mexico.

The model reached R² values of 0.91, 0.95, and 0.99 respectively against the GRACED inventory.

Tested against a completely independent dataset – ODIAC, which derives emissions from nighttime light imagery and power-plant data at 1 km resolution – it still scored between 0.90 and 0.99.

Four countries, two independent benchmarks, consistent accuracy.

Something unexpected emerged from the mobility data. The Louvain community detection algorithm carved China’s 366 cities into 11 functional clusters.

These are groupings defined not by provincial borders but by how people actually move between them. Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei formed one cluster, pumping out 62.75 million kilograms of carbon daily.

The Yangtze River Delta formed another, at 49.71 million.

These clusters aren’t just descriptive. More central, more connected clusters emit more carbon.

But here’s the policy hook. China’s existing climate governance tends to target a handful of major emitting cities while overlooking smaller ones that sit in structurally critical positions within the network.

The mobility-defined clusters offer something different: a template for coordinated regional decarbonization that matches how economies actually function rather than how administrative maps happen to be drawn.

The authors aren’t overselling this. They call mobility a “partial but observable proxy” – a complement to inventories, not a replacement.

The Chinese analysis covers a single extraordinary two-month window. The data captures intercity movement, not what happens within a city.

Mobility alone may not fully capture emissions changes driven by seasonal energy demand, holiday schedules, or weekly cycles.

There are subtler problems too. Cellular signaling data inherits all the biases of telecom coverage – regional disparities, operator market share, sampling artifacts.

And the fundamental link between mobility and emissions could shift as remote work spreads, transport electrifies, and travel patterns reshape.

A correlation forged during the most dramatic behavioral disruption in modern history might not hold the same way during a quiet Tuesday in 2030.

Still, the core appeal is hard to argue with. Standard emissions inventories are accurate but glacially slow.

With timely access to mobility data, the framework could provide frequently updated emissions estimates.

If it scales, climate policymakers would gain a behavior-informed reading of the present rather than a months-old accounting of the past.

The team calls for fusing their mobility approach with remote sensing, energy structure data, and meteorological variables.

The ambition is to make carbon monitoring something closer to weather forecasting: imperfect, always updating, but fast enough to actually be useful.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

#6365. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

D. Ancalle et al. Earwax as pest control. Soft Matter. 2026. https://doi.org/10.1039/d6sm00737f

#6363. Webb reveals the hidden activity inside a turbulent stellar nursery

Webb peers through thick cosmic dust in NGC 7129, revealing hidden young stars, protostars, glowing gas, and powerful outflows.

Today’s Image of the Day from the European Space Agency reveals a stellar nursery where young stars are changing the clouds that gave birth to them.

The James Webb Space Telescope captured NGC 7129, a star-forming region about 3,300 light-years from Earth.

Thick clouds of gas and dust obscure much of the activity at visible wavelengths.

Webb’s infrared vision can penetrate that material, bringing previously hidden stars and structures into view.

The result shows much more than a collection of newborn stars. NGC 7129 contains objects at several stages of early stellar development.

Some are still gathering material. Others have moved closer to the long, stable period of life that includes stars such as our Sun.

Stars do not all mature at the same rate. More massive stars generally form and evolve faster than smaller ones.

That difference allows astronomers to study several chapters of stellar development within the same region.

The brightest central star in this scene is LkH(alpha) 234. It has about five to eight times the mass of the Sun and produces the image’s most noticeable diffraction pattern.

It is a pre-main-sequence star, meaning it has largely finished collecting mass but has not yet begun the sustained hydrogen fusion that will define its main-sequence life.

At this stage, gravity continues to pull the star inward. As it contracts, its interior grows hotter.

Eventually, conditions in the core will become intense enough for hydrogen fusion to begin.

This transition matters because a young star does not develop quietly.

Even before reaching the main sequence, it can send powerful streams of material into the gas around it.

Those outflows can reshape a stellar nursery across surprisingly large distances.

The clearest evidence appears to the left of LkH(alpha) 234. A golden cavity stretches roughly 3.5 light-years across.

Outflows produced during an earlier stage of the star’s development carved into the surrounding molecular cloud, which consists largely of hydrogen.

Radiation and outflowing material from the star energize the gas and make it glow.

Some gas gets swept away, but the process does not simply shut down star formation.

Other material becomes compressed. Dense pockets can then provide the conditions needed for additional stars to develop.

Several young stars are visible inside the cavity. Some are also pre-main-sequence stars, and they produce stellar winds of their own.

As these winds push into surrounding gas, they create curved structures called bow shocks.

The stars also create a hot environment beside colder, denser molecular material. The boundary between these environments is known as a photodissociation region.

Energetic radiation breaks hydrogen molecules apart into individual atoms there.

The process changes the chemistry, heating and cooling of the cloud and helps determine how it evolves.

Molecular clouds are the raw material for star formation, but the stars born inside them gradually help destroy them.

Radiation, winds, and outflows can disperse gas or alter its chemistry.

Over millions of years, those effects can erode the cloud and change where new stars are able to form.

NGC 7129 gives astronomers a particularly useful view of that process because its stars have reached different developmental stages.

Their combined activity shows how star formation can both disrupt a cloud and compress parts of it into conditions favorable for further stellar growth.

The right side of Webb’s image tells an earlier part of the story.

Clumpy red material conceals protostars that are younger than the pre-main-sequence stars visible elsewhere in the region.

Protostars form after cold molecular gas and dust collapse and fragment into dense concentrations.

They continue gaining mass from surrounding material.

At the same time, they can eject narrow, extremely hot outflows that slam into the dense matter around them.

Those collisions produce shocks within the gray material surrounding the protostars.

They help create the textured appearance seen by Webb and contribute to the region’s red glow.

Several protostars are active at once, so their outflows overlap from Earth’s viewpoint. That makes this side of NGC 7129 look especially tangled.

Yet the apparent disorder contains valuable information about stars that would otherwise remain hidden behind dust.

Infrared observations give astronomers access to these deeply embedded objects before they emerge from their birth clouds.

In NGC 7129, Webb captures stars at different points along that path while also revealing how strongly they affect their surroundings.

The nursery will continue changing as its young stars mature.

Gas will disperse, dense pockets may collapse, and some newly formed stars will eventually settle into the hydrogen-fusing stage that powers the Sun today.

Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Maya used so much red paint that they accidentally poisoned their lakes and waterways with mercury, a new study finds.

The problem was cinnabar, a vivid-red mercury-sulfide mineral that can be used as the pigment vermilion in red paint. The run-off from the paint can enter waterways, where anaerobic bacteria then transform cinnabar into highly toxic methylmercury in the sediments of lakes. Over time, the methylmercury accumulates to higher levels in the food chain.

The ancient Maya, a people who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America and whose descendants are still around today, painted almost everything red. Archaeologists have found countless artifacts that the Maya reddened, including sculptures, monuments, walls, plazas, pottery and the dead for ceremonial funerals. Cinnabar was a common pigment in the paint they made, along with red ocher, which gets its color from a nontoxic iron mineral called hematite.

But the Maya passion for the color red — which to them represented the sun, blood and life — caused an environmental disaster when the nearby waters were poisoned by the cinnabar runoff, said study first author Matthew Waters, a paleolimnologist (a scientist who studies ancient waterways) at Auburn University in Alabama.

"They would have seen a strange color change in the water … and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein," he told Live Science. The Maya depended heavily on freshwater fisheries, including for freshwater shellfish.

Previous studies had already found evidence for high levels of mercury in the Maya's southern highlands and south-central lowlands, but no one had fully examined levels of the toxic mineral in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

To investigate, Waters and his colleagues studied mercury levels in Maya-era mud in the Yucatán, and found overwhelming signs of mercury poisoning, probably from cinnabar paint, they reported in their study, published Nov. 4 in the journal Science Advances.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We did not suspect [the Maya] used it in the quantities that we were seeing," he said.

The study found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores from two Maya-era sites: Cobá Lake, a shallow lake beside the Maya city of that name, and Cenote Xcach (also spelled X-Canché), a flooded sinkhole beside a ruined city in the jungle that few have excavated.

The sediment cores chronicle the composition of earth and water over more than 2,000 years, and the times of mercury poisoning coincide with several periods during the Preclassic and Classic periods of the Maya civilization from about A.D. 40 to 820.

Waters explained that the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. has determined it is unsafe to drink water with mercury levels above 2 parts per billion, while the official limit for the level of mercury in fish, where it builds up over time, is 1 part per million — any number above that means the fish can be seized by authorities.

Severe poisoning occurs when the mercury levels in human blood exceed about 100 parts per billion, from drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated marine animals, such as fish. In humans, mercury poisoning can cause severe symptoms, including permanent lung damage, brain damage and death.

The reddish hue of the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, made between the sixth and ninth centuries, now housed in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology, shows the Maya's love for mercury.

The most polluted parts of the Yucatan cores had a mercury level of 2.3 parts per million, the team discovered. "They experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries," Waters said.

The researchers then examined the sediment cores for signs of environmental damage caused by the mercury poisoning. They found that the cores lacked tiny fossils of freshwater shellfish, indicating that the high mercury levels were killing marine life. The team also noticed that the sediment cores had hardly any traces of algal blooms, which should have happened frequently, Waters said. That's likely because algae could not survive in the poisoned water nutrients.

Scholars debate why the Maya civilization collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries, but a leading suspect is the disruption of food supplies caused by drought.

But although mercury levels were high during the Preclassic and Classic periods, the environmental damage caused by mercury levels had been falling in many places for hundreds of years by the time of the Maya collapse, Waters said, although it may have been a contributing factor.

Cinnabar does not occur naturally in the Yucatán, so it must have been imported there, probably from what's now Honduras, the researchers said. It seems these cinnabar imports eventually stopped at Cobá Lake, and the poisoning there fell to a background level of about 20 parts per billion by A.D. 520. However, the sediment cores showed that the mercury poisoning continued at Cenote Xcach until the collapse, they said.

Waters, M. N., Wooten, S. L., Abrook, A. M., Brenner, M., Curtis, J. H., Langdon, P. G., Medina-Gonzalez, R. M., Paradeisis-Stathis, S., & Vachula, R. S. (2026). Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya. Science Advances, 12(45), eaeh3280. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh3280

#6361. MIT researchers built a tiny new computer from squishy materials that works like a human brain

A soft film 2 nanometers thick lets a tiny device hold a memory for seconds and then fire like a neuron, all within one part.

Computers left moving parts behind a long time ago, trading gears and wheels for electrons flowing through chips that don’t change shape.

At a size far smaller than a single brain cell, a new device goes back to motion. Once squeezed, it takes a few seconds to recover its shape, so it can add up signals and fire, like an artificial neuron.

Because of that delay, one tiny part holds a short memory and acts on it. That job usually takes extra components such as capacitors.

Farnaz Niroui, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of its Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), led the team that built it. Chemist Jeremiah Johnson of MIT’s Department of Chemistry joined them.

It’s a laboratory demonstration, and its biggest energy savings are a projection rather than a measurement.

Part of the inspiration came from animals that handle information where it arrives. For example, many of an octopus’s nerve cells are in its arms, which can sense and respond without waiting on the brain.

“You can think of an octopus as continuous computing matter, with computing, memory, sensing, and actuation distributed throughout its body,” Niroui said.

Mechanical computing goes back at least to the gears of the ancient Antikythera mechanism.

Modern mechanical computers have mostly stayed at the scale of millimeters. Shrinking them further runs into a basic problem. Surfaces brought within a few billionths of a meter of each other pull together and stick.

To get around it, the researchers laid a soft polymer film called PDMS, about 2 nanometers thick, between two gold electrodes.

Each device’s working area is a square 200 nanometers on a side, so more than 20 of them could fit across even a small neuron.

The top electrode is free to move. When the researchers applied a voltage, the two electrodes pulled toward each other and squeezed the film. More current crosses a thinner gap, so the current rose as the film thinned.

Niroui described the film as a “nano-spring” that keeps the metal surfaces from collapsing together for good. From the current, the team calculated that the gap shrank from about 2.3 nanometers to 1.6 nanometers.

They confirmed the squeeze with light. As the voltage rose, light scattered off a device shifted toward red, while a copy built with a stiff ceramic layer instead of PDMS showed no shift.

Peter Satterthwaite, a graduate student who co-led the work with fellow graduate student Sarah Spector, explained why that matters.

“PDMS is viscoelastic, which means that after being compressed, it takes time to return to its original state,” Satterthwaite said.

“This allows the devices to dynamically remember the history of forces and voltages applied to them, and convert that history into an electrical response.”

A pulse lasting 50 milliseconds squeezed the film by about 8 percent, and the current recovered as soon as the voltage stopped. A pulse 10 times longer squeezed it by about 30 percent, and the current returned gradually over several seconds.

So what the device does now depends on what happened to it a few seconds ago. When the team waited only half a second between tests instead of 40 seconds, the film hadn’t fully recovered, and the tests started from a narrower gap.

A neuron in the brain collects incoming signals a little at a time. If they arrive slowly, the charge drains away. If they arrive close together, the charge builds past a threshold, and the neuron fires a signal to its neighbors before resetting.

The neuron device did the same thing. The team sent it a string of 2.5-volt pulses, each too weak to trigger it alone, spaced closer together than the film could recover. After 16 pulses, the current jumped, and the device then relaxed back to where it started.

“We have this complex functionality, which is the basis of biological computing, all contained in one nanoscale device,” he said.

Its memory lasts seconds, while most other artificial neurons hold theirs for millionths or thousandths of a second. The team wrote that this suits tasks that need context over a few seconds.

The researchers also wired two devices to one shared resistor. Once the first device fired, the second couldn’t fire until the first had relaxed, the way one active neuron in a brain can hold back its neighbor.

As built, the device used 54 nanojoules of energy in tests. By the team’s calculation, it only needs to store about 2 femtojoules of electrical energy each time it fires, and a femtojoule is a millionth of a nanojoule.

At 200 nanometers across, the device is more than 100 times smaller than a typical neuron. Cut the current that leaks through it and shrink it further, the team wrote, and it could beat a real neuron on energy efficiency.

The team presented that kind of efficiency as a way to meet the growing demands of artificial intelligence.

“The performance highly relies on the memory introduced using the soft polymer,” Spector said. “We can intentionally engineer this over a large design space to meet the requirements of the desired applications.”

Every measurement was made in a lab, on devices kept under nitrogen gas at 80 percent humidity, and the devices held up better in humid conditions than dry ones. Devices from separate batches behaved alike but not identically.

The team showed single devices and one connected pair, not a network trained to do a task. The authors wrote that practical use will take progress on the materials, the device design and the training methods.

Spector said the material could also suit devices that work with the body, such as prosthetics that process touch quickly or low-power health patches worn on the skin. The team also mentioned robots and environmental sensors.

Next, the team wants to build sensing into the same material, so a single squeezable layer can sense, remember and compute.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6359. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”
