#6308. How to Watch the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade

As the turkey thaws and a day of cooking prep begins, an equally integral Thanksgiving tradition is Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Last year, 3.5 million spectators lined New York City’s streets to watch the procession of vibrant balloons and whimsical floats bob and weave through Midtown Manhattan to the beats of countless marching bands and celebrity performers. Beyond the city, a record-setting 34.3 million tuned into the NBC and Peacock broadcast, making the Emmy-winning production the year’s most-watched entertainment telecast. This year's promises to be even grander, as 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the spectacle, which started in 1924 (though it wasn’t held from 1942 to 1944 because parade materials were reserved for wartime efforts).

“As a kid from the Bronx, it is an honor to bring this cherished tradition…to the city of New York every year,” the parade’s executive producer since 2021 Will Coss tells Condé Nast Traveler. The annual highlight for him is seeing the joyful expressions of spectators of all ages as the parade passes them by “showcasing some of the most iconic and recognizable pop culture characters and figures.”

This year marks the 99th anniversary of the Macy's Parade, an annual Thanksgiving tradition.

On the eve of the parade's centennial, the team—composed of painters, carpenters, animators, sculptures, welders, designers, engineers, and electricians—is honoring its past by way of revived classics like Felix the Cat and Underdog balloons. Ardent fans will also find a swath of newcomers that include a Fantasia-inspired Mickey, cowboy Minion, and a Peanuts duo. “The team at Macy’s Studios works year-round to make this historic parade bigger and better for our audiences every year,” Coss says. Here’s everything you need to know about the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026—all its surprises, delights, and familiar joys.

When Macy’s first debuted its one-million-square foot New York City flagship store at 34th Street between Broadway and Seventh Avenues in 1924, the retailer threw a Christmas parade on Thanksgiving morning to boost holiday sales—with a much longer route starting at 145 Street and Covent Avenue. Balloons joined the lineup in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat, and the festivities were first broadcast nationally in 1947.

These days, the festive parade follows a 2.5-mile path from the Upper East Side to Midtown Manhattan. Starting at the corner of 77th Street and Central Park West, the route heads south to Columbus Circle and then turns east, heading along 59th Street to Sixth Avenue. From there, it goes straight down Sixth Avenue to 34th Street, ending in front of Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square.

Clifford the Big Red Dog in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Coss recommends arriving early for a great view. Many spectators start to gather as early as 6 a.m. along the beginning of the route on Central Park West (approach from the west) from 61st to 75th Streets. Other prime spots include the south side of 59th Street between Columbus Circle and Sixth Avenue and the entire stretch of Sixth Avenue between 38th and 59th. Spectators should be aware there is no viewing on Central Park West between 59th and 60th Streets, or anywhere south of 38th Street.

Coss also reminds those bringing children to dress warmly for the chilly weather and to be prepared to entertain young ones for a few hours while waiting to spot the first float. He suggests avoiding strollers, large bags, backpacks, and umbrellas.

In celebration of its centennial, some 100 inflatables will fly. Returning after decades are much-anticipated Felix the Cat (the parade's first character balloon, introduced in 1927) and Blue Hippopotamus (from the 1931 parade), while Hello Kitty and Underdog (who appeared in every parade from 1965 through 1984) will also make cameos. New to the scene are Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, and Snoopy persona Joe Cool with Woodstock, among others. The procession will also welcome 52 floats, 31 clown crews, nine specialty units (such as trycaloons, or balloons ridden on tricycles), seven marching bands, and five balloonicles (that’s a balloon-vehicle hybrid).

TODAY’s Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker will host the live broadcast of the 100th Macy’s Parade. Though this year's performance lineup has yet to be announced, the 2025 roster featured 26 celebrity performers, ranging from Colbie Caillat and Christopher Jackson to Foreigner and Taylor Momsen, complete with a performance by KPop Demon Hunters’ HUNTR/X singing voices EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and Rei Ami. As anticipation for the parade's centennial only increases, Coss says this year will “bring new surprises and delights to the iconic holiday tradition and truly celebrate this incredibly special anniversary.”

For some, the majestic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an official marker of the transition into the Christmas season in New York City.

Americans can watch the live telecast on both NBC and Peacock on Thursday, November 26, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones, while Telemundo will air a Spanish-language simulcast hosted by Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz, and Clovis Nienow. For late risers, an encore will air starting at 2 p.m. ET/PT, and the full broadcast will also be on NBC with live audio description on Secondary Audio Program channel (SAP). Behind-the-scenes footage will be shared on social media @macys and #MacysParade via Instagram, TikTok, and Threads.

To rev up for the turkey day excitement, “Countdown to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” will air on Wednesday, November 25, on NBC and Peacock. The primetime special will broadcast live from the parade starting line with exclusive previews and behind-the-scenes stories from the balloons and floats.

One of the most underrated—and free—ways to experience the parade is by attending the Thanksgiving Eve balloon inflating event on Wednesday, November 25, a “time-honored tradition and special peek into the parade celebrations,” Coss says. Since 1994, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has invited guests to see the process the balloons undergo to reach their larger-than-life size and scale the afternoon before Thanksgiving. Last year’s took place between 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., with the line opening at noon.

Those interested can enter at West 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, where they’ll be guided through a security checkpoint and then can roam between West 77th and 81st Streets to view the balloons. Note that prohibited items include bags or backpacks larger than 12-by-6-by-12 inches, lawn chairs, large coolers, alcoholic beverages, chairs, weapons, drones, pets, and umbrellas; participants will be screened before entering the route.

For the latest up-to-date information, visit macys.com/parade for details on the parade and nbc.com/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade for updates on the broadcast.

A 2019 astronaut photo shows the near-perfect cone of a highly active volcano poking its heavily scarred and partially snow-covered head above a thick bank of low-lying clouds over the Kuril Islands.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Atlasov Island, off the coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula [50.84755357, 155.56126752]

What's in the photo? The summit of Alaid volcano peeking above a thick layer of low-lying clouds

Who took the photo? An unnamed astronaut on board the International Space Station

This eye-catching astronaut photo shows a towering, highly active Russian volcano poking its head above a thick bank of swirling clouds over the Kuril Islands.

The lofty peak is located on Atlasov Island, the northernmost of the Kuril Islands — a chain of roughly 50 largely uninhabited volcanic landmasses stretching along a fault line that runs between Russia and Japan in the Sea of Okhotsk. Altasov lies 40 miles (65 kilometers) off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, which is also renowned for its volcanic activity.

The island consists mainly of a single, massive volcano, called Alaid, which is known for its near-perfect cone shape. Alaid reaches up to 7,497 feet (2,285 meters) above sea level, making it the tallest peak in the Kuril Islands.

Alaid has erupted at least nine times in the past 50 years, including a major outburst in April 1981 that ejected a 1,250-mile-long (2,000 km) plume of thick smoke and ash into the atmosphere, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

Its most recent eruption occurred between September and November 2022, when a river of lava flowed down its flank (see below). During this outburst, the volcano also spit out smoke and ash that was spotted from space alongside another eruption plume coming from the nearby island Paramushir.

Alaid last erupted in November 2022 and unleashed a scorching lava flow down its snow-covered slopes. This photo also shows what Atlasov Island looks like when it is not obscured by clouds.

In the astronaut's photo, roughly half of Atlasov Island rises above a deep, low-lying bank of swirling clouds. The summit of Alaid, crowned by a roughly mile-wide (1.6 km) caldera, is also obscured by clouds. (The volcano was not erupting when the photo was taken.)

Farther down the volcano's flanks are a series of snow-filled gullies carved out by lava flows from previous eruptions. Eagle-eyed viewers may also be able to spot some parasitic cones — small openings where lava burst through in the past — around the edge of the cloud layer, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The area surrounding a cluster of parasitic cones on the volcano's northwest flank (top right in the photo) is devoid of vegetation ‪—‬ a result of another major eruption in 1972, which scoured the surrounding landscape with hot ash. A 2009 study revealed fresh signs of recovery in the affected area, but noted that it could take hundreds of years for vegetation to return to pre-eruption levels.

The clouds are not the only thing the island rises above. Alaid is essentially the summit of a much larger underwater volcano that lies beneath the Sea of Okhotsk. The rest of the island has grown around the exposed cone as lava flows have reached sea level and solidified. Millions of years ago, this larger volcano was likely connected to the Kamchatka Peninsula via a land bridge that has since been submerged.

In 1981, a major eruption caused Alaid to unleash a massive plume of smoke and ash that reached up to 1,250 miles long.

Astronauts and satellites have snapped several other stunning shots of intriguing landmasses nearby, including a quartet of end-to-end volcanoes on Simushir Island and a set of volcanic "nesting dolls" on Onekotan Island.

And in 2022, the Landsat 8 satellite also spotted the iconic summit of Mount Vesuvius peeking through a gap in the clouds over Italy, just like Alaid.

A 2024 astronaut photo shows the icy surface of Pangong Lake breaking apart in the lofty Tibetan Plateau. The point where the ice meets the water almost perfectly matches a disputed border between China and India.

A 2020 astronaut photo shows the unique structure of Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active stratovolcano in Tanzania that was recently adorned with a bright white "ash cone." The explosive peak produces a rare type of lava that is unusually cool but travels remarkably quickly.

A 2010 satellite photo shows the point where a small lake bisects the snowy rim of an ancient glacier on Canada's Baffin Island. The rippling, snow-rimmed structure is the last remaining fragment of a colossal ice sheet that once covered large parts of North America.

#6305. Airport Luggage Tag Scam: How to Protect Your Checked Bags in 2026

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and says, “Then why is your name on it?”

That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

Baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

We have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an update.

In 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

This may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

When you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

In the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

That is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

Most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger issue is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

That is true in Toronto. It is true in New York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

International travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

The Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

That is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

Yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

This video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

This matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

You are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that says this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

Make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

You are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

Keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

That receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

You do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

The important thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

Trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

We use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

Make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag quickly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

But do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that says, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

Check that it is actually yours. Look at the tag, compare the bag number against your receipt, check your tracker, inspect the condition, and make sure the contents have not obviously been disturbed.

We have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

Not necessarily. We have traveled for decades, and carry-on only is not always realistic. Sometimes you need to check a bag, especially on longer trips, family trips, cruises, cold-weather destinations, camera-heavy travel, or extended international travel.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

The point is not to scare people out of checking luggage. The point is to update your habits.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

That’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

So before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

The goal is not to travel scared. The goal is to travel smarter.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.

#6304. 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter

If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing. We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate, or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues.

From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England, these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away.

Where are you staying? Mayflower Inn & Spa, Washington, Connecticut

What drew you to this hotel? I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design.

What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County, a region beloved by many of my colleagues. Next time I visit the hotel, I’ll have to make a few stops along the way to see what all the fuss is about.

Where are you staying? Urban Cowboy Lodge, Big Indian, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Urban Cowboy Lodge has been on my weekend getaway wish list for years, and there’s something about it in winter that feels particularly charming—maybe it’s the delightful snow-filled view from the bathtub (pictured above) that drew me in. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city.

What are you eating? Phoenicia Diner, of course. I’m also keen to try out some of the many craft beers at Ralph’s Bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I’m not a skier, so in the winter, heading to the Catskills comes with more of a stay-indoors-and-get-cozy vibe for me. Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley.

Where are you staying? The Rockaway Hotel & Spa, Rockaway Park, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Aside from the ocean views—poetically perfect for New York in the winter—The Rockaway is home to one of my favorite wellness scenes in the city. The space transforms its outdoor pool area (which, in the summer months, is home to outdoor concerts and DJ-led pool parties) into the cozy Winter Pool House. The space gets decked out with outdoor cedar barrel saunas and the softest plush robes to wear while you transition to the heated outdoor pool. The warm water mixed with the ice-cold breeze coming off the nearby coastline is glorious.

What are you eating? I’ll be heading to Margie’s—the mood-lit hotel lobby restaurant—and ordering a juicy cheeseburger and a frosty gin martini. What better way to warm your soul?

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The beauty of visiting this hotel in winter? No summer beach crowds. I’ll likely bundle up, head to the beach for some meditation, and head right back to my cozy room at The Rockaway to soak up the views even more.

Where are you staying? Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection, Gardiner, New York

What drew you to this hotel? I’ve had Wildflower Farms on my wish list for the past few years. Every photo I see of the property on Instagram looks so dreamy. It feels like a true escape from the city—quiet, cozy, and restful. Located in New York’s Hudson Valley, it’s a quick 90-minute drive from NYC, making it a convenient pick for couples or families seeking an easy getaway.

What are you eating? I’m most eager to have coffee and pastries around the fire at the Great Porch, Wildflower’s open-air communal space with sprawling views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And of course, I’ll be dining at the resort’s on-site restaurant, Clay, where the rustic American menu is full of seasonal ingredients from local farms.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I usually try to pack as many activities and must-try coffee shops and restaurants as possible into my trip itinerary, but Wildflower Farms encourages you to slow down. You’ll find me at Thistle, the resort’s on-site spa where hand-harvested, small-batch oils and scrubs are used during tailored treatments.

Where are you staying? Inness, Accord, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Inness is resplendent in the summer, so I’ve always been keen to see a different side of it come hunker-down weather. Its cabins are certainly primed for rest, thanks to the fireplaces, but there’s also the outdoor pit with prime-time views of the Catskill Mountains decked in snow. I also love the central farmhouse, where cozy seats call out for a great book and a hot cocoa. And if you can drag yourself out, which you should, there are loads of hikes and walks, including those along the Ashokan Reservoir, which is one of my favorite spots.

What are you eating? Stacks of pancakes; comfort-food entrées like risottos; a round of Dorato Negronis at the bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Spending the afternoons shopping and dining in some of my favorite nearby towns, like Kingston and Woodstock.

Where are you staying? Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club, Surfside, Florida

What drew you to this hotel? When one of my best friends announced she was celebrating her 30th birthday in Miami, a city I’ve shockingly never been to, the first place I thought of was the Four Seasons Hotel at the Surf Club; I remember reading about its incredible celebrity guest history, which includes everyone from Frank Sinatra to Elizabeth Taylor.

What are you eating? Perhaps we’d start with a toast at the on-site Champagne Bar, then move on over to dinner at Lido for seafood-inspired pastas.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Laze around by the pool, enjoy the quieter beaches of Surfside, and maybe stroll through the Rubell Museum in Allapattah.

Where are you staying? Tourists, North Adams, Massachusetts

What drew you to this hotel? I love heading north of the city in the colder months—leaning in and getting even colder and cozier. And the words “reimagined motor lodge” are another form of catnip for me. I love the sense of nostalgia paired with very plush, updated interiors, ideal for hiding out for a wintery weekend.

What are you eating? I’d carve out time for the hotel’s restaurant, the Airport Room, ideally timed to one of the chef pop-ups they do—though given the three-and-a-half-hour drive from New York City, I’d probably also plot out an en route lunch in Kingston as well.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Wintery hikes on the nearby trails, lots of reading by the fireplace, and maybe some of the arts and crafts activities—why not.

Where are you staying? Eastwind, Windham, New York

What drew you to this hotel? When I first caught sight of Eastwind, I was really into the property’s sprawl—there are different types of accommodations (cabins, hotel-style rooms), and everything is wound together via a small trail system lined with fairy lights, from the beer garden to the main house. It feels like a really great spot to get away from the noise of New York City.

What are you eating? The on-site restaurant, Dandie’s, serves up barbecue in a cozy, window-lined space—get some house-made gelato for dessert. And definitely make a detour for brunch at Phoenicia Diner on your way back to the city.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Stop by Harriman State Park for a hike to stretch your legs on the way north. Once you’re there, you’ve got skiing options (Windham Mountain Club), more hiking trails (The Windham Path), and indoor activities (Helsinki Hudson for music lovers; Olana Historic Estate for museum enthusiasts).

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6303. The 8 Best Battery Packs Keep Your Gadgets Going

Top off your phone, tablet, laptop, or any other gadget without dropping everything to sit by an outlet.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s 2026, and everyone should have a portable battery pack in their bag, backpack, purse, or jacket pocket. We all keep at least a couple of battery-powered gadgets on us every day, including a phone, a pair of headphones or earbuds, and maybe a smartwatch. And that’s before we get into the stuff we bring to and from work every day, like laptops, tablets, handheld game consoles, and e-readers. Your battery pack is like a security blanket for your tech. It allows you to go through your day knowing that you will always have access to all your devices—even if they run out of power, you have the ability to charge them up on the spot. As a tech reporter, I never leave home without one.

And, conveniently, it doesn’t cost much to add one of these EDC tech essentials to your arsenal. Though large packs with the juice to fully recharge your laptop can get a bit pricey, you can get a pocket-sized pack to top off your phone throughout the day from a reliable brand for as little as $30 to $40. We’ve been testing these gadgets for years and have some thoughts on which ones are worthy of a spot in your bag or your pocket.

I’ve carried a battery pack on me every day for more than a decade, going back to the early 2010s, when most gadgets had modest capacities and needed at least one extra charge to get through the day. While batteries have improved, both in our devices and the battery packs, I always have one handy and am usually testing a new one or two in search of a new favorite.

For this guide, I pored over product listings and sifted through specs to find the packs with the newest features and best “estimated” performance, then spent weeks with each selection as my backup power source on the go. Whether you’re a creative pro who keeps a whole tech arsenal on hand at all times or just someone who travels a lot and needs to make sure their phone is always on, there are options on this list that will fit into your life.

The ReelCharge ReelPro 200W is the perfect ready-for-anything charger. Furnished with a 140W USB-C charging cable, plus two additional ports, this 27,000mAh laptop charger can keep all of your EDC tech powered up about as well as plugging directly into an outlet.

For reference, 140W of charging output on a single device is very fast. In 2026, most laptop charging cables can’t hit that speed. So forget about worrying whether or not your battery pack can actually charge your laptop: Now you may find yourself wishing your normal power brick could keep up.

Though not quite as impressive, it’s worth noting that 27,000 mAh is about as large a capacity as you can expect to see from a battery pack: FAA regulations ban batteries larger than 100 watt-hours, and this cuts close to that limit. There are plenty of other laptop chargers that meet the restriction, but this one packs it into a relatively compact form factor.

Not everyone loves having built-in cables in their power banks, but the feature is a must in my book. It saves time and lets you charge devices (and the pack) without worrying about whether you have an extra cable handy.

I also love that it has a built-in color screen, which lets you monitor its charging level, the power input or output of its ports, and all-around battery health. Like the onboard cable, this feature is a must in the mid-2020s and far better than the LED indicator lights of older battery packs.

The Anker Zolo offers ample 20,000-mAh battery capacity, stellar charging speeds, and abundant connectivity features that are on par with our top pick, another Anker battery. But this one is extremely cheap—less than $50. It doesn’t have the charging capacity to support high-end laptops like a MacBook Pro, but it should work wonders with just about anything else.

Having a pair of integrated USB-C cables whose braided covers match its exterior (in black, white, blue, and pink) makes the Zolo look more upmarket than the price suggests, as does the accessory’s digital display. It doesn’t show as much information as the screens on Anker’s top packs, but it is still a nice touch and rare at this price.

Anker also offers a lower-priced version of the Zolo with only one USB-C cable, which is perfect if you’re singularly focused on charging your phone.

At under $25, this highly portable pack from Baseus is the cheapest pack I’ve used and am confident recommending. With a maximum power output of 22.5 watts, the Baseus EnerFill can juice up a modern smartphone to around 50 percent in about half an hour. Its charging speed lags behind our other picks, but that's a fair trade-off, given the price.

Light and easy is the name of the game, here: It weighs just over 7 ounces and connects to devices via a built-in USB-C cable and a pair of additional ports. It even has a little flourish in the form of a digital display that gives you a more precise look at battery level than the usual pip-based indicator. Throw in a two-year warranty, and this is an incredible bargain.

The Anker Nano is, as the name implies, designed to be ultraportable. As you can see, Anker knows how to make a battery pack, and this one comes with many of the design flourishes I love in the best overall pick, including a retractable USB-C cable and a color display.

The difference here is that this is pocket-sized and made to support smaller gear. In this case, though, “smaller” really just means everything but the most heavy-duty tech. With a 10,000-mAh battery pack and a maximum power output of 45 watts, it can rapidly power up any phone and tablet. It can also extend the screen time of compact notebooks like the MacBook Air. It’s not suitable for MacBook Pros, however.

This is a solid compromise for folks who want a lot of charging power but need a smaller charger, or want to keep their budget under $60.

In a crowded field of magnetic battery packs designed to snap to the back of an iPhone or a top-shelf Android phone, I’ve come to rely on the Sharge Icemag 3 because of its original design, fast wireless speed, and some unique special features.

It supports Qi 2.2, the latest wireless charging standard, which can deliver up to 25-watt output. When you plug in its integrated USB-C cable, that speeds up to 35 watts, which is enough to top off some lightweight laptops.Beyond the basics, the Icemag 3 has some interesting extra features, including a sturdy kickstand, and an onboard cooling fan to help it maintain consistent charging speeds. Most magnetic battery packs want to fade into the background, but the Icemag 3 has the look and the feature-set to stand out and make a strong impression.

If you’re going backpacking and you need a battery pack that can take a little bit of punishment, we like Nestout’s rugged offering. Its shockproof exterior and IP67 rating for water and dust resistance mean it’s ready for long camping trips where it might spend a little time in the dirt. The ports also feature screw caps with tight seals, providing complete protection between charges.

With a 15,000-mAh battery capacity, three charging ports, and a maximum power output of 32 watts, this version of the battery pack offers a fine balance between speed and versatility. Smaller Nestout power banks with capacities of 10,000 and 5,000 mAh are also available. All battery packs are compatible with additional accessories, including a solar charger and an attachable USB light.

The Powerstation Mini is the most compact pack I’d consider using regularly and truly lives up to its “mini” moniker. It's just a tad larger than a tube of lipstick and slips easily into the smallest pocket in your jeans or a clutch purse. And thanks to a sleek aluminum shell, it doesn’t look like a tech accessory when not in use.

There is a price for its minuscule footprint, though—slower charging speed. Still, this is more than fine for juicing up your phone or a pair of earbuds in a pinch.

The Anker Prime sets itself apart from other laptop-grade battery packs with its retractable wall plug. It may sound like overkill, but having one unlocks higher power output to charge or power large laptops and other, less portable devices.

I like the battery pack’s sleek design, with a built-in color screen that displays vital information about the charging process and its remaining capacity. As a final throw-in, it comes with a very nice braided USB-C cable.

Needless to say, there are a lot of battery packs out there, and for every one that I’ve recommended here today, my fellow editors and I have tested many alternatives. Honestly, as long as you’re sticking with brands with a reputation for quality, the difference between our picks and the next best thing is pretty small: Either they cost a bit more than the competition for a similar offering, or charge at a slightly slower rate. In a couple of cases, they’re legitimately just as good, but fill a niche that not many people need. Here are a few highlights from our most recent tests:The latest run of battery packs from battery pack founding father Mophie includes the Powerstation Plus Mini 5K and, the Powerstation Plus 10K, as well as the Powerstation Plus Signature Series Mini 5K and Powerstation Plus 10K. In attempting to make battery packs for every price point, the brand has stretched its offerings too thin. The standard Powerstation Plus packs are genuine bargains at $30 and $40, but lack competitive charging speeds and features. The Powerstation Signature Series packs have faster rates (though not the fastest we’ve tested), and braided cables, which make them more durable. If the Signature Series packs were priced like the Standard Series, they’d be shoo-ins for the list. As is, they lack a superlative spec on which to hang their hats.

We’ve also tested a new raft of battery packs from Ecoflow, a brand you may be familiar with if you’ve read our guide to solar generators. The most recent options from the brand’s “Rapid” power bank series all feature 45W fast-charging, which is faster than average for a small to mid-size pack. Senior Commerce Editor Mike Epstein says the best of the bunch, the Rapid 20K, is pretty remarkable: You get a lot of power and fast charging for less than $50. The pack is a bit large, though: It’ll fit in your pocket, but maybe not comfortably. Ecoflow also makes a number of novel options, like the Rapid 10K 3-in-1 charger, which can do double duty as both wall charger and power bank. Like the Rapid 20K, it’s an interesting pack. Either one of these could earn a spot on our list one of these days, because their performance and price are very appealing, but we’re keeping them here for now because they fill a more specialized niche than any of our current picks.Lastly, we should highlight the Nimble Sharepower, an interesting 10,000 mAh power bank that can split apart into two 5,000 mAh packs, so two people can charge devices independently. Again, it’s a niche pick aimed at parents looking to keep their kids’ iPad charged without sacrificing their own backup power. At $80, it’s a bit pricey for what it is. (You can buy two 5,000 mAh packs for less.) But if you can see it being useful, this is a unique choice that could be a lifesaver for the person, in the right situation.

Capacity is the be-all, end-all of any battery (or battery pack), as it determines how much power your device can store. Typically measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), the higher your battery pack’s capacity is, the more power it has to distribute to your devices throughout the day.

Keep in mind, though, that a larger capacity almost always means a larger, heavier, and more expensive battery pack. As you can see from our picks, there are good reasons to buy different packs with different capacities based on what you plan to charge, and how you plan to carry it.

For most people, I recommend looking for a pack around 10,000 mAh, which should be portable enough to fit in your pocket and have enough juice to charge your phone a couple of times, or a smaller device four times or more. This should be enough to get your essential EDC gadgets through a day of extremely heavy use (like when you’re traveling), or a long weekend off-grid.

If you are carrying a laptop, a digital camera, or a large number of devices that all need charging from time to time, you should probably scale up to a larger “laptop charger” battery pack that can hit 20,000 mAh or more. The limit here is usually 25,000 to 28,000, as most manufacturers want to keep the battery under the FAA’s 100-watt-hour battery capacity limit for passenger airliners. (If you’re looking for something bigger that doesn’t need to fly, consider our guide to portable power stations.)

Capacity is the obvious and highly publicized metric for battery packs, but it is often power output that separates the good chargers from the bad ones. Output, measured in watts (w), tells you how fast the battery pack can charge your devices. The actual speed will also depend on the output supported by the device it’s charging. But a faster battery pack will be helpful, especially with larger, more expensive gear.

For most people, I recommend getting a battery pack that delivers at least 45 watts of power from a single output. That’s enough to rapidly charge phones and ultraportable laptops like the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air. Faster options are few and far between, and you’ll only need them for large devices like a MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop.

That said, many battery packs don’t hit that speed, and I wouldn’t immediately dismiss them out of hand. The smaller your pack’s capacity, the less likely you’ll need a fast-charging pack. Try to look for 30 watts in a compact power bank, but even less than that is okay for pocket-sized options, especially if it’s a slim, wireless charging pack that attaches directly to a phone.

It’s important to note that using a battery pack to charge multiple devices often slows down charging across each device. Depending on the construction, the pack’s maximum output can be spread across one or many ports. While shopping, keep an eye on the output of each port. And when you’re charging, keep in mind that you should only charge one device at a time when time is of the essence.

Unless the power bank you’re eyeing is super tiny like the Mophie I recommend above, look for a device with an integrated USB-C cable. Having the wire built in is super convenient. You can use it to charge devices and replenish the power bank itself. More than one built-in cable is preferable for larger power banks.

Additional USB-C outputs are also mandatory for a battery pack, unless it’s super tiny—again like the Mophie Powerstation Mini already mentioned. An old-school USB-A port is also great to have, just in case, especially on larger power banks.

Julie Elie, an ethologist at the University of California, Berkeley, tells Live Science's Kenna Hughes-Castleberry about using AI to decode the vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. #6301. The Best Frame TVs Bring a Discreet, Tasteful Look to Your Living Room

These alternative screen designs feature matte, anti-glare displays that make static art look just as good as your favorite movie.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Unlike conventional TVs, which display a black screen when powered off, frame TVs display museum-quality artwork, family photos, and other media. With customizable bezels in various materials and colors, they look like picture frames and blend better with your home’s aesthetic.

While early frame TVs were all style and no substance, the technology behind these displays has evolved significantly. Today’s models feature matte screens that reduce glare, brightness sensors that automatically adjust to ambient lighting, and advanced display technologies that match the best 4K TVs on the market.

When shopping for a frame TV, factors like screen size, display quality, and style play a role just as they would with the best gaming TVs. However, frame TVs introduce additional considerations. Some premium models offer interchangeable bezels in various materials, while installation is a bit more challenging. They may also include free access to curated galleries, though some require monthly subscriptions. Below, we’ll dive into all the features to consider when searching for a solid frame TV, along with a few recommended picks.

For this roundup, I established clear criteria that each TV had to meet to qualify as a true “frame TV.” First and foremost, they had to have an elevated design beyond the traditional black rectangle—a design that can blend into your existing décor. Second, each model needed a dedicated art mode with specialized screen technology—like anti-glare—that minimizes reflections. Lastly, I considered options with some form of customization, including interchangeable bezels and curated art libraries. Samsung’s The Frame earns our top recommendation for effectively pioneering this category, offering a beautiful design, matte display, and extensive art collection. That said, each model in this roundup offers unique advantages. Whether you’re looking for a premium art display, a design statement, or a more budget-friendly option, our selections cater to various preferences and price ranges.

Samsung’s The Frame made a splash when it debuted in 2017, creating a TV that perfectly disguised itself as a piece of art. A few generations later, the TV looks even better and has the technology to match. The 2025 model brings years of refinement, featuring a QLED 4K display, an anti-reflective matte coating, and quantum dot technology that delivers vibrant colors and deep contrast.

The Frame’s anti-glare coating gives the TV a canvas-like appearance, so you can place it in a bright room without the picture washing out. When the art mode is activated, the matte finish helps diffuse ambient light, creating the illusion that you’re standing before an actual painting in a gallery. Samsung’s adaptive brightness sensor further enhances this effect by automatically adjusting the display’s brightness to match the room’s lighting conditions throughout the day.

Additionally, the TV features a built-in motion sensor that detects when you enter or leave the room, automatically turning its art mode on/off to save power. The Frame further helps save energy by lowering its refresh rate from 120 Hz to 60 Hz when art mode is activated. To help eliminate cable clutter, The Frame comes with an external hub that houses all the TV’s ports and connections, so you can hide everything from view.

Samsung's Art Store, which provides access to more than 2,000 curated works of art, requires a monthly subscription. Meanwhile, the TV's customizable bezels are sold separately and typically range from $100 to $200, depending on size and material. This can add to the overall cost of the TV, which already comes at a premium.

TCL’s frame TV line, Nxtvision, brings the art display concept to a more accessible price point while still offering advanced features such as a 4K QLED display, a high refresh rate, and next-generation gaming capabilities. At just 1.1 inches deep, the Nxtvision TV is incredibly thin, and it comes with a mount so it sits flush against the wall.

Like other options on this list, it features an anti-glare screen, which creates a convincing paper-like look, maintaining the illusion of physical artwork. The TV’s processor can also optimize color, contrast, and clarity, ensuring you get the best picture quality no matter what’s being displayed.

In addition to a curated gallery featuring various styles and periods, there’s an AI art capability that generates custom artwork from prompts. Additionally, you can display your personal photo gallery, giving you a huge picture frame for your favorite memories. The only drawback is that the Nxtvision comes with its own proprietary mount, so it’s not VESA-compatible, which may limit your mounting options.

If you’re in the market for another value pick that doesn’t scream “technology” when not in use, the Hisense CanvasTV is a mid-range lifestyle TV with an art mode that showcases Renaissance paintings, family photos, and more. Its matte display reduces reflections and gives artwork more depth and texture, so pictures look like actual paintings.

Additionally, the ultra-slim wall mount lets you hang it flush against the wall for that coveted gallery look. The magnetic frame system (teak comes standard) also lets you easily change the look of the CanvasTV to match your décor. Just note that it only comes in just two sizes, 55 and 65 inches, limiting placement options.

The CanvasTV doesn’t sacrifice performance for aesthetics, delivering an excellent picture with its 4K QLED display. Gamers will also appreciate the 144 Hz refresh rate and Auto Low Latency Mode, ensuring smooth gameplay without screen tearing or motion blur. Together, the combination of design and features makes the CanvasTV an excellent value.

The LG G5 isn’t necessarily a gallery TV like Samsung’s The Frame, but it features a slim design with a barely noticeable bezel, plus a gallery mode for showcasing artwork and photos. For these reasons, and others, including best-in-class picture quality, we believe this pick is a good entry point for those who want to upgrade their current model to a hybrid lifestyle TV.

On the G5’s OLED display, images look stunning thanks to perfect blacks, infinite contrast, and vibrant colors. It also offers better brightness—a major weakness of OLED—with some clever engineering that helps the screen stay vivid. However, as good as the OLED display is, it can still appear slightly washed out in bright ambient light, which may influence where you place it in your room.

While it doesn’t offer customizable bezels like The Frame, the LG G5’s minimalist aesthetic naturally complements modern interiors without sticking out like a sore thumb. Without a stand, the TV is just 1 inch thick, creating a sleek, floating appearance that doesn’t protrude from your wall.

Beyond its aesthetics, this pick also offers excellent functionality. Its four HDMI 2.1 ports allow you to enjoy gaming at 4K resolution with a smooth 120 Hz refresh rate. Dolby Vision support ensures that movies look their best, and Filmmaker Mode helps preserve the director’s original vision, providing the optimal viewing experience.

As frame TVs have grown in popularity, their size range has increased, too. When Samsung’s The Frame launched in 2017, it was available in only a few sizes. But now, the TV is available in sizes ranging from 32 inches to 85 inches. Frame TVs from other manufacturers also come in a variety of sizes, allowing you to get the option that best fits in your space.

When you’re shopping for a frame TV, I recommend resisting the urge to go for the largest size you can afford. Instead, think about how far you’ll be sitting from the screen. A huge TV in a small room can actually make viewing uncomfortable, because you’ll need to constantly move your eyes across the screen to take in all the action—it’s like sitting too close to a theater screen.

On the flip side, a TV that’s too small can force you to squint to make out details. Finding the sweet spot is crucial, especially with frame TVs designed to blend seamlessly with your décor. That sweet spot will vary depending on the available space, décor, etc., but generally, you should measure the area where you plan to place the TV before purchasing it.

Whether you’re shopping for a premium TV or something more affordable, there are different display technologies you should know about, including QLED and OLED. In the TV space, QLED is a common option among top manufacturers. This technology employs quantum dots to enhance color vibrancy and brightness, making it perfect for viewing art or pictures throughout the day.

Meanwhile, OLED is still widely regarded as the best display technology because of its ability to deliver true blacks and infinite contrast. Each individual pixel is self-emitting, meaning it can turn completely off when displaying black, providing a stunning viewing experience for high-contrast content.

While OLED is making its way into some high-end frame TV options, it offers lower peak brightness than QLED. This can make content appear less vibrant in well-lit rooms, so it's worth considering if you’d like to display bright content on your TV.

While frame TVs are generally wall-mounted, they come in a few installation styles. Wall mounting creates the illusion that your TV is a picture frame (hence the name), allowing it to hide in plain sight.

Most manufacturers include the appropriate mounting hardware, but the customizable bezels that allow you to match your TV’s frame to your décor are typically sold separately. This extra hardware generally comes in different wood tones and colors to best match your taste.

While a frame TV mostly serves as a decorative piece, there are a few extra features that sweeten the deal. Most models include dedicated art modes featuring curated galleries with thousands of classic and contemporary artworks.

However, if you want to access the full galleries with artwork from the world’s leading museums and artists, you may have to pay a subscription fee. For example, Samsung’s The Frame requires a subscription to its art store to access more than 2,000 iconic images

Frame TVs also incorporate auto-brightness features that use built-in sensors to detect your room’s ambient light. These sensors automatically adjust the screen brightness, similar to how smartphones adapt their displays between indoor and outdoor environments.

Many models also include motion sensors that detect when someone enters the room, automatically activating the display to show artwork without requiring you to turn the TV on manually. Additionally, frame TVs typically incorporate anti-glare technology that reduces reflections, creating a more authentic, canvas-like appearance.

Brandon Russell is a freelance writer covering gear and technology. He started his journey as a news writer at a small newspaper and later began reviewing smartphones, movies, and video games. In his free time, he enjoys the slower, more intentional experience of using a 35mm film camera and making short videos about movies he grew up watching.
